body.text: Dharmakīrti: Hetubindu
body.translated_text: <s>Dharmakīrti</s>: <s>Hetubindu</s> (A Drop of Reasons)

body.text: namo buddhāya /
body.translated_text: Homage to the <s>Buddha</s>.

body.text: (1.1) parokṣārthapratipatteranumānāśrayatvādeva tad vyutpādanārtha saṃkṣepata idamārabhyate- pakṣadharmastadaṃśena vyāpto hetustridhaiva saḥ / avinābhāvaniyamād hetvābhāsāstato 'pare //
body.translated_text: (1.1) Since the apprehension of imperceptible objects depends on inference (<s>anumāna</s>), this [work] is commenced in brief for the purpose of explaining that: The property of the thesis-subject (<s>pakṣadharma</s>), pervaded by a portion of that [thesis-property], is the reason (<s>hetu</s>), and it is of three kinds only. Due to the restriction of invariable concomitance (<s>avinābhāva</s>), the pseudo-reasons (<s>hetvābhāsa</s>) are the others [beyond these three]. ||

body.text: (1.2) pakṣo dharmī, avayave samudāyopacārāt / prayojanābhāvādanupacāra iti cet / na / sarvadharmidharmapratiṣedhārthatvādupacārasya / evaṃ hi cākṣuṣatvādi parihṛtaṃ bhavati / dharmavacanenāpi parāśrayatvād dharmasya dharmyāśrayasiddhau pratyāsatteḥ sādhyadharmiṇa eva siddhiriti cet / na / pratyāsatteḥ dṛṣṭāntadharmiṇo 'pi / siddhe tadaṃśavyāptyā dṛṣṭāntadharmiṇi sattve punardharmiṇo vacanaṃ dṛṣṭāntadharmiṇa eva yo dharmaḥ sa heturiti niyamārthamāśaṃkyeta / dṛṣṭaṃ sajātīya eva sattvam ityavadhāraṇena sādhyābhāve siddhe 'pi vyatireke sādhyābhāve asattvavacanam, tathehāpi tadaṃśavyāptivacanāt siddhe 'pi dṛṣṭāntadharmiṇi sattve tatraiva bhāvaniyamārtha dharmivacanamāśaṃkyeta / tasmāt sāmarthyād arthapratītāvapi upacāramātrāt samānanirdeśāt pratipattigauravaṃ ca parihṛtaṃ bhavati /
body.translated_text: (1.2) The thesis (<s>pakṣa</s>) is the property-bearer (<s>dharmin</s>), through the figurative application of the whole to its part. [Objection:] There is no figurative application due to the absence of purpose. [Reply:] No, because the figurative application serves to exclude all [other] properties from the property-bearer. For in this way, properties such as being perceptible to the eye (<s>cākṣuṣatva</s>) and the like are excluded. [Objection:] Even with the mention of "property" (<s>dharma</s>), since a property depends on something else, in establishing its dependence on the property-bearer, due to proximity, only the property-bearer of the <s>sādhya</s> (probandum) is established. [Reply:] No, because due to proximity, the example's property-bearer (<s>dṛṣṭāntadharmin</s>) [is established] as well. When existence in the example's property-bearer is established through pervasion by a portion of that, the additional mention of the property-bearer might be suspected to restrict that only the property of the example's property-bearer is the reason (<s>hetu</s>). Just as, when the negative concomitance is already established by the restriction "existence is observed only in the homogeneous [class]," the statement of non-existence in the absence of the probandum [is made]; so here too, when existence in the example's property-bearer is already established through the statement of pervasion by a portion thereof, the mention of the property-bearer might be suspected to restrict existence to that alone. Therefore, even when the meaning is understood through [logical] capacity, through mere figurative application and equal designation, the difficulty of comprehension is also avoided.

body.text: (1.3) pakṣasya dharmatve tadviśeṣaṇāpekṣasyānyatrānanuvṛtterasādhāraṇateti cet / na / ayogavyavacchedena viśeṣaṇāt / yathā caitro dhanurdhara iti / nānyayogavyavacchedena / yathā pārtho dhanurdhara iti / tadaṃśastadharmaḥ /
body.translated_text: (1.3) [Objection:] Since the property of the thesis depends on its qualifier and does not recur elsewhere, it is uncommon (<s>asādhāraṇa</s>). [Reply:] No, because the qualification is through exclusion of wrong connection (<s>ayogavyavaccheda</s>), as in "<s>Caitra</s> is an archer." Not through exclusion of other connections (<s>anyayogavyavaccheda</s>), as in "<s>Pārtha</s> is an archer." A portion of that [thesis] is its property.

body.text: (1.4) tasya vyāptirhi vyāpakasya tatra bhāva eva / vyāpyasya vā tatraiva bhāvaḥ / etena anvayo vyatireko vā pakṣadharmaśca yathāsvaṃ pramāṇena niścita uktaḥ / sarvatra hetau sādhyavaidharmye vyāptyasiddhervyāpakānivṛttau nivṛttyabhāvādvā / anvayavyatirekāniścayābhyāṃ hi taddharmavyāptiniścayaḥ /
body.translated_text: (1.4) For the pervasion (<s>vyāpti</s>) of that is indeed the presence of the pervader (<s>vyāpaka</s>) therein, or the presence of the pervaded (<s>vyāpya</s>) only therein. By this, positive concomitance (<s>anvaya</s>) or negative concomitance (<s>vyatireka</s>), and the property of the thesis-subject, each ascertained by its respective means of valid knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>), are stated—because in every case the pervasion is not established when there is dissimilarity with the probandum in the reason, or because there is no cessation when the pervader does not cease. For the ascertainment of the pervasion of that property is [achieved] through the ascertainment of positive and negative concomitance.

body.text: (1.5) tatra pakṣadharmasya sādhyadharmiṇi pratyakṣato 'numānato vā prasiddhiḥ / tathā pradeśe dhūmasya, śabde vā kṛtakatvasya /
body.translated_text: (1.5) There, the property of the thesis-subject is established in the subject of the probandum through <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) or through <s>anumāna</s> (inference)—just as smoke [is established] in a location, or the property of being produced (<s>kṛtakatva</s>) in sound.

body.text: sadhūmaṃ hi pradeśamarthāntaraviviktarūpamasādhāraṇātmanā dṛṣṭavataḥ smārtaṃ yathādṛṣṭabheda viṣayaṃ liṅgajñānamutpadyate /
body.translated_text: For one who has perceived a location with smoke—in a form distinct from other things, with its unique character (<s>asādhāraṇātman</s>)—there arises an inferential cognition based on memory, having as its object a differentiation as [previously] perceived.

body.text: tatra yadādyamasādhāraṇaviṣayaṃ darśanaṃ tadeva pramāṇam /
body.translated_text: There, that initial perception which has the unique particular as its object is itself the <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge).

body.text: (1.6) tasmiṃstathābhūte darśanena dṛṣṭesati sa yena yenāsādhāraṇastadasādhāraṇatāṃ tato bhedamabhilapantī atadvayāvṛtiviṣayā smṛtirutpatrā pratyakṣabalena na pramāṇam / yathādṛṣṭākāragrahaṇāt, prāgasādhāraṇaṃ dṛṣṭvā asādhāraṇa ityabhilapataḥ apūrvārthādhigamābhāvāt, arthakriyāsādhanasya ālocanājñānena darśanācca / adṛṣṭasya punastatsādhanasya vikalpenāpratipatteranumānavat /
body.translated_text: (1.6) When that [particular] in such a form has been perceived through direct perception, the memory that arises—referring to the exclusion from what is not that (<s>atadvyāvṛtti</s>), expressing its distinction from whatever makes it unique—is not a <s>pramāṇa</s> by the force of direct perception: because it grasps the form as [previously] perceived; because there is no apprehension of a new object for one who, having first perceived the unique, then expresses "unique"; and because the object capable of efficient action (<s>arthakriyāsādhana</s>) is perceived through the apprehending cognition (<s>ālocanājñāna</s>). But for something not [directly] perceived, there is no apprehension of that efficient object through conceptual construction (<s>vikalpa</s>), as in the case of inference.

body.text:
arthakriyārthī hi sarvaḥ prekṣāvān pramāṇamapramāṇaṃ vānveṣate / na ca sāmānyaṃ svalakṣaṇapratipatterūrdhvaṃ tatsāmarthyotpatravikalpavijñānagrāhyaṃ kāñcidarthakriyāmupakalpayati / yathā nīlaṃ dṛṣṭvā nīlamiti jñāne / tadeva hi nīlasvalakṣaṇaṃ tathāvidhasādhyārthakriyākāri / tacca tenātmanā dṛṣṭameva ālocanāpratyayena /
na ca tatsvalakṣaṇagrahaṇottarakālabhāvino nīlavikalpasya viṣayeṇa nīlasādhyārthakriyā kriyate /
body.translated_text: For every discerning person who seeks efficient action (<s>arthakriyā</s>) investigates whether [something] is a valid means of knowledge or not. And the universal (<s>sāmānya</s>), grasped by conceptual cognition (<s>vikalpavijñāna</s>) arising through the capacity of that [perception] beyond the apprehension of the particular (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>), does not accomplish any efficient action. Just as when one sees blue and has the cognition "it is blue"—for it is the particular of blue itself (<s>nīlasvalakṣaṇa</s>) that accomplishes the desired efficient action of that kind, and that has been perceived in its own nature through the apprehending cognition (<s>ālocanāpratyaya</s>). And the efficient action pertaining to blue is not accomplished by the object of the conceptual construction of blue that arises after the grasping of that particular.

body.text: (1.7) tasmāt anadhigatārthaviṣayaṃ pramāṇam ityapi anadhigate svalakṣaṇe iti viśeṣaṇīyam / adhigate tu svalakṣaṇe tatsāmarthyajanmā vikalpastadanukārī kāryatastadviṣayatvāt smṛtireva, na pramāṇam, anadhigatavasturūpasyānadhigateḥ / vastvadhiṣṭhānatvāt pramāṇavyavasthāyāḥ / arthakriyāyogyaviṣayatvāt tadarthināṃ pravṛtteḥ / arthakriyāyogyalakṣaṇaṃ hi vastu / tato 'pi vikalpāt vastunyeva tadadhyavasāyena puruṣasya pravṛtteḥ / pravṛttau pratyakṣeṇābhinnayogakṣematvāt /
body.translated_text: Therefore, even the [definition] 'a <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid cognition) has as its object something not yet cognized' must be qualified as [meaning] 'when the <s>svalakṣaṇa</s> (unique particular) has not yet been cognized.' But when the <s>svalakṣaṇa</s> has been cognized, the conceptual cognition (<s>vikalpa</s>) born from the capacity of that [perception], being an imitation of it, is merely <s>smṛti</s> (memory) — since it has that [previously perceived object] as its content through the causal relation — and not a <s>pramāṇa</s>, because the real nature of the object that has not been [previously] cognized is not [newly] cognized [by it]. For the establishment of <s>pramāṇa</s> is grounded in real objects (<s>vastu</s>). Because the activity of those who seek a [particular] end is directed toward objects capable of causal efficacy (<s>arthakriyāyogya</s>). For a real entity (<s>vastu</s>) is defined as that which is capable of causal efficacy (<s>arthakriyā</s>). Even from that conceptual cognition, a person acts toward the real entity alone, through the determination of it [as the object]. Because in [producing successful] activity, [conceptual cognition] has no different outcome than direct perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>).

body.text: pūrvapratyakṣakṣaṇena abhinnayogakṣematvāduttareṣāṃ kvacidaprāmāṇyaprasaṅga iti cet / na / kṣaṇaviśeṣasādhyārthavāñcāyāṃ nānāyogakṣematvāt / sādhāraṇe hi kārye na teṣāṃ sāmarthyabhedaḥ / aparāparadhūmapramitasatrikṛṣṭāgniṣu iva anumānajñānānāmagnimātrasādhye 'rthe / etena dharmidharmaliṅgādivikalpasya pramāṇapṛṣṭhabhāvinaḥ prāmāṇyaṃ pratyuktam /
body.translated_text: [Objection:] If [conceptual cognition] has no different outcome from the first perceptual moment, it would follow that subsequent [perceptions] are not <s>pramāṇas</s> in some cases. — [Reply:] No, because when the desired end requires a particular moment, there are different outcomes. For with respect to a common effect, there is no difference in their capacity — just as inferential cognitions [arising from] successive [perceptions of] smoke, regarding fires already cognized as existent, [are all valid] when the end to be achieved is merely fire [in general]. By this, the validity of the conceptual cognition of the property-bearer (<s>dharmin</s>), the property (<s>dharma</s>), the logical mark (<s>liṅga</s>), etc. — which arises subsequent to the <s>pramāṇa</s> (<s>pramāṇapṛṣṭhabhāvin</s>) — is also explained.

body.text: (1.8) anvayaniścayo 'pi svabhāvahetau sādhyadharmasya vastutastadbhāvatayā sādhanadharmabhāvamātrānubandhasiddhiḥ / sā hi sādhyaviparyaye hetorbādhakapramāṇavṛttiḥ / yathā sat tat kṣaṇikameva, akṣaṇikatve 'rthakriyā virodhāt tallakṣaṇaṃ vastutvaṃ hīyate /
body.translated_text: The ascertainment of positive concomitance (<s>anvaya</s>) in the case of the essential nature reason (<s>svabhāvahetu</s>) is the establishment that the property to be proven (<s>sādhyadharma</s>) is invariably connected with the mere existence of the proving property (<s>sādhanadharm</s>), because it is in reality of the same nature as it. For that [positive concomitance] is [established by] the operation of a sublating cognition (<s>bādhaka-pramāṇa</s>) for the reason in the absence of the <s>sādhya</s>. For example: whatever exists is necessarily momentary (<s>kṣaṇika</s>), because if it were non-momentary, causal efficacy (<s>arthakriyā</s>) would be contradicted, and [thus] its reality (<s>vastvuta</s>), defined by that [causal efficacy], would be negated.

body.text: kāryahetau kāryakāraṇabhāvasiddhiḥ / yathedamasyopalambhe upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptamanupalabdhamupalabhyate, satsu apyanyeṣu hetuṣu asyābhāve na bhavatīti yastadbhāve bhāvastadabhāve 'bhāvaśca pratyakṣānupalambhasādhanaḥ kāryakāraṇabhāvaḥ tasya siddhiḥ / kāryakāraṇabhāva eva hyarthāntarasya evaṃ syāt- yatra dhūmastatrāvaśyamagniriti, agnibhāva eva hi bhāvo dhūmasya tatkāryatvamiti /
body.translated_text: In the case of the effect reason (<s>kāryahetu</s>), [it is] the establishment of the cause-effect relation (<s>kāryakāraṇabhāva</s>). For example: when this [entity] is perceived, that which fulfills the conditions of perceptibility (<s>upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta</s>) but was previously unperceived is [now] perceived; and when, even though other causes are present, in the absence of this [entity], that [effect] does not occur — such presence [of the effect] when [the cause] is present and absence when [the cause] is absent, established through perception and non-perception, constitutes the cause-effect relation; its establishment [is what is meant here]. For only the cause-effect relation could account for [the invariable connection with] something else thus: 'wherever there is smoke, there is necessarily fire' — for the existence of smoke is precisely [its] being in the state of fire [i.e., being produced by fire], which is its being an effect of that [fire].

body.text: anupalabdhāvapi anvayaniścayaḥ asadvayavahārasyopalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptasyānupalabdhimātravṛtti sādhanaṃ, nimittāntarābhāvopadarśanāt /
body.translated_text: In non-perception (<s>anupalabdhi</s>) too, the ascertainment of positive concomitance [is as follows]: the means of establishing the convention of non-existence (<s>asadvyavahāra</s>) operates through the mere non-perception of what fulfills the conditions of perceptibility (<s>upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta</s>), because no other cause [for such convention] is observed.

body.text: (1.9) vyatirekaniścayo 'pi kāryasvabhāvahetvoḥ kāraṇavyāpakānupalabdhibhyāṃ dṛśyaviṣayābhyāṃ kāryakāraṇavyāpyavyāpakabhāvasiddhau satyāṃ sādhyābhāve 'bhāvasiddhiruddiṣṭa viṣayasyābhāvopadarśane / anupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptasyānyathā kvacidabhāvāsiddheḥ / anuddiṣṭaviṣayaṃ sādhyābhāve hetvabhāvakhyāpanaṃ pratibandhamātrasiddhau sidhyatīti na tatra vyatirekasādhane anupalabdhyoḥ dṛśyaviṣayatāviśeṣaṇamapekṣyate / vyatirekāniścayo 'nupalabdhāvupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptāt sato 'nupalambhābhāvadarśanam /
body.translated_text: The ascertainment of negative concomitance (<s>vyatireka</s>) in the case of the effect and essential-nature reasons [is established] through non-perception of the cause and the pervader (<s>vyāpaka</s>) — both having perceptible objects — when the cause-effect and pervaded-pervader relations have been established: the establishment of [the reason's] absence in the absence of the <s>sādhya</s> [operates] through demonstrating the absence of the specified object, because otherwise the absence [of the reason] somewhere could not be established for what fulfills the conditions of perceptibility. The announcement of the reason's absence in the absence of the <s>sādhya</s> with respect to an unspecified domain is accomplished through the mere establishment of the necessary connection (<s>pratibandha</s>) — therefore, in that case, the qualification that the non-perceptions have perceptible objects is not required for proving negative concomitance. The non-ascertainment of negative concomitance in the case of non-perception is the observation that there is no non-apprehension of what exists and fulfills the conditions of perceptibility.

body.text: (1.10) etallakṣaṇaḥ tridhaiva saḥ hetustriprakāra eva / svabhāvaḥ kāryamanupalabdhiśceti / yathā anitye kasmiṃścitsādhye sattvamiti / agnimati pradeśe dhūma iti / abhāve ca upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptasyānupalabdhiriti / atraiva trividhahetāvavinābhāvasya niyamāt / pakṣadharmasya yathoktā vyāptiravinābhāvaḥ / na sa trividhāddhetoranyatrāstītyatraiva niyata ucyate /
body.translated_text: Having these characteristics, the reason (<s>hetu</s>) is of three kinds only — threefold indeed: <s>svabhāva</s> (essential nature), <s>kārya</s> (effect), and <s>anupalabdhi</s> (non-perception). For example: when something impermanent is to be proven, [the reason is] existence (<s>sattva</s>); [when] fire [is to be proven] in a location, [the reason is] smoke; and in [proving] absence, [the reason is] the non-perception of what fulfills the conditions of perceptibility. Because the invariable concomitance (<s>avinābhāva</s>) is restricted to these three kinds of reason alone. The <s>vyāpti</s> (pervasion) of the property of the thesis (<s>pakṣadharma</s>) as stated is the invariable concomitance. It is said to be restricted to these alone, because it does not exist in any reason other than the threefold reason.

body.text: (2.1) tatra sādhanadharmabhāvamātrānvayini sādhyadharme svabhāvo hetuḥ / aparāparavyāvṛttibhedena dharmabhede satyapi vastutaḥ liṅgasvabhāva eva / hetusvabhāve sādhyadharme 'nvayavyabhicārābhāvāt lakṣaṇe tanmātrānvayeneti viśeṣaṇaṃ paramatāpekṣam /
body.translated_text: Among these, the essential nature reason (<s>svabhāvahetu</s>) is [the one] where the property to be proven (<s>sādhyadharma</s>) is positively concomitant with the mere existence of the proving property (<s>sādhanadharm</s>). Even though there is a difference in properties through the distinction of different exclusions (<s>vyāvṛtti</s>), in reality [the <s>sādhya</s>] is of the very nature of the logical mark (<s>liṅga</s>). The qualification 'concomitant with that alone' in the definition [is stated] because there is no deviation in positive concomitance when the <s>sādhyadharma</s> is of the nature of the <s>hetu</s>; [this qualification] is with regard to the opponent's position.

body.text: pare hi arthāntaranimittamatadbhāvamātrānvayinamapi svabhāvamiccanti / tena ca viśeṣaṇena tathavidhasya atatsvabhāvatāṃ tasmin sādhye hetorvyabhicāraṃ cāha / yathā hetumati vināśe kṛtakatvasya /
body.translated_text: For the opponents hold that even [a property] which is caused by something else and is merely concomitant with what is not of its nature alone is also an essential nature [reason]. By that qualification, [<s>Dharmakīrti</s>] states both the non-essential-nature-hood of such [a purported reason] and its deviation (<s>vyabhicāra</s>) with respect to that <s>sādhya</s>. For example, [the property of] being produced (<s>kṛtakatva</s>) in [proving] destruction that has a cause.

body.text: (2.2) tasya dvidhā prayogaḥ / sādharmyeṇaikaḥ vaidharmyeṇāparaḥ / yathā yat sat tat sarvaṃ kṣaṇikam / yathā ghaṭādayaḥ / saṃśca śabdaḥ iti / tathā, kṣaṇikatvābhāve sattvābhāvaḥ saṃśca śabda iti / sarvopasaṃhāreṇa vyāptipradarśanalakṣaṇau sādharmyavaidharmyaprayogāvuktau /
body.translated_text: (2.2) The application of that [inference] is twofold: one by positive concomitance (<s>sādharmya</s>) and another by negative concomitance (<s>vaidharmya</s>). For example: "Whatever exists is entirely momentary, like pots and the like; and sound exists." Likewise: "In the absence of momentariness, there is absence of existence; and sound [exists]." The applications through positive and negative concomitance, characterized by the demonstration of <s>vyāpti</s> (pervasion) through complete enumeration, have [thus] been stated.

body.text: (2.3) atra pakṣadharmasambandhavacanamātrasāmarthyādeva pratijñārthasya pratīteḥ na pratijñāyāḥ prayoga upadarśitaḥ / apradarśite prameye kathaṃ tatpratītiriti cet / svayaṃ pratipattau prameyasya ka upadarśayitā? pradeśasthaṃ dhūmamupalabdhavataḥ tasyāgninā vyāpteḥ smaraṇe tatsāmarthyādeva agniratra iti pratijñārthapratītirbhavati / na ca tatra kaścit agniratreti asmai nivedayati / nāpi svayamapi prāgeva pratipadyate kiñcit, pramāṇamantareṇaivaṃ pratīteḥ nimittābhāvāt pratītau liṅgasya vaiyarthyam / svayamevākasmāt agniratreti vyavasthāpya tatpratipattaye paścālliṅgamanusaratīti ko 'yaṃ pratipatteḥ kramaḥ? pareṇāpi taducyamānaṃ plavata eva upayogābhāvāt / viṣayopadarśanamupayoga iti cet, tenaiva tāvaddarśyamānena ko 'rthaḥ? yadi pratītiranyathā na syāttadā sarvaṃ śobheta / tasmādeṣa svayaṃpratītau kenacid viṣayopasthāpakena vināpi pratiyan asmān kāryiṇo dṛṣṭvā parvabrāhmaṇa iva vyaktaṃ mūlyaṃ mṛgayate / asmadvacanādapi svayaṃ siddhameva liṅgamanusṛtya sādhyaṃ pratyetīti ko 'nayoravasthayorviśeṣaḥ? dṛṣṭā ca pakṣadharmasambandhavacanamātrāt sādharmyavatprayogādeḥ pratijñāvacanamantareṇāpi pratītiriti kastasyopayogaḥ? svaniścayavadanyeṣāmapi niścayotpādanāya sādhanamucyate / tatra svayaṃ prameyopadarśanena vināpi pratipadya paraṃ pratipādayatrapūrva kramamāśrayate iti kimatra kāraṇam? tasmātra prameyasya vacanena kiñcitprayojanamanyathāpi pratipatterutpatteḥ /
body.translated_text: (2.3) Here, since the understanding of the meaning of the thesis (<s>pratijñārtha</s>) arises from the mere capacity of the statement of the connection of the property of the subject (<s>pakṣadharmasambandha</s>), the application of the thesis has not been demonstrated [as a separate member]. — [Objection:] If the object to be proved (<s>prameya</s>) is not shown, how can there be understanding of it? — [Reply:] In self-cognition, who is the demonstrator of the object to be proved? For one who has perceived smoke situated in a place, upon the remembrance of the pervasion of that [smoke] by fire, through just that capacity, the understanding of the thesis-meaning — "there is fire here" — arises. And no one there informs him "there is fire here." Nor does he himself understand anything beforehand [without the inferential mark]; for in the absence of a cause for such understanding without a means of valid knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>), the inferential mark (<s>liṅga</s>) would be purposeless in producing cognition. That he himself, without any [prior] cause, first establishes "there is fire here" and then afterwards follows the inferential mark for understanding that — what kind of order of cognition is this? Even when stated by another, that [thesis statement] merely floats [without purpose], due to the absence of any use. — [Objection:] If it is said that its use is the presentation of the subject matter — then what is the point of it being shown by that [thesis statement] alone? If the understanding could not arise otherwise [without the thesis statement], then everything [said in its defense] would be justified. Therefore, this [opponent], even though understanding arises by itself without any presenter of the subject matter, seeing that we have some task [to accomplish], like a <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> at a festival, seeks a manifest price [for unnecessary services]. Since even from our statement, one cognizes the <s>sādhya</s> (what is to be proved) by following the inferential mark which is itself self-established, what difference is there between these two situations? And since understanding is observed even without a thesis statement, from the mere statement of the connection of the property of the subject, through the application of positive concomitance and the like — what use does [the thesis statement] have? The proof is stated in order to generate certainty in others just as in one's own [case]. There, since one oneself understands even without the demonstration of the object to be proved and then demonstrates it to another — why would one resort to this unprecedented procedure? Therefore, here there is no purpose in the verbal statement of the object to be proved, since understanding arises even otherwise.

body.text: (2.4) etenopanayanigamanādikamapi pratyuktam / etāvataiva sādhyapratīterbhāvāt / ḍiṇḍikarāgaṃ parityajyākṣiṇī nimīlya cintaya tāvat kimiyatā pratītiḥ syātra veti / bhāve kiṃ prapañcamālayā? iti iyāneva sādhanavākye prayogo jyāyān /
body.translated_text: (2.4) By this, [the need for] application (<s>upanaya</s>), conclusion (<s>nigamana</s>), and so forth is also refuted, since the understanding of what is to be proved arises from just this much. Setting aside partisan attachment, close your eyes and consider: would understanding arise from just this much or not? If it does, what need is there for an elaborate garland [of additional members]? Therefore, just this much application in the proof-statement is the best.

body.text: (2.5) atra pūrvaṃ hetuḥ prayoktavyaḥ paścād dṛṣṭānta iti kramaniyamo 'pi na kaścit / sarvathā gamakatvāt /
body.translated_text: (2.5) Here, there is also no fixed rule of sequence that the reason (<s>hetu</s>) should be stated first and the example (<s>dṛṣṭānta</s>) afterwards, since [the proof] serves as a means of understanding in every arrangement.

body.text: (2.6) sambandhavacane 'pi nārthabhedo 'pi kaścit / ubhayathāpi tadbhāvasyaiva khyāpanāt / nahi atatsvabhāvasya bhāve ekāntenānyasya bhāvaḥ kṛtakatvasya bhāve prayatnānantarīyakatvavat / kāryasyāpi atatsvabhāvasyābhāve na tannivṛttiḥ, yathānayoreva naikanivṛttāvanyanivṛttiḥ /
body.translated_text: (2.6) Even in the statement of the relation [as positive or negative concomitance], there is no difference in meaning whatsoever, since in both ways it is the existence of that [invariable relation] alone that is made known. For it is not the case that when that which is not of a certain nature is present, there is invariably the existence of another [property] — just as, in the presence of being-produced (<s>kṛtakatva</s>), there need not be the property of being-immediately-preceded-by-effort (<s>prayatnānantarīyakatva</s>). Nor does the absence of an effect that is not of that nature entail the cessation of that [other thing] — just as, regarding these two [properties] themselves, the cessation of one does not entail the cessation of the other.

body.text: tasmādanvayavyatirekayoryathālakṣaṇameko 'pi prayokto dvitīyamākṣipatīti naikatraṃ sādhanavākye dvayoḥ prayogaḥ iṣyate vaiyarthyāt / tatsvabhāvatayānvayasiddhau tadabhāve 'bhāvo 'pi sidhyatyeva / tathā siddhau cānvayasyāpi siddheriti / tadabhāva eva hetorabhāvakhyātiryathā syāt nānyatra vipakṣe viruddhe vā iti niyamakhyāpanārtho 'pi vyatirekaprayogo na yuktaḥ, anyaviruddhayorapi vipakṣatvāt /
body.translated_text: Therefore, since [from among] positive concomitance (<s>anvaya</s>) and negative concomitance (<s>vyatireka</s>), even one stated according to its definition implies the other, the application of both in a single proof-statement is not desired, due to redundancy. When positive concomitance is established through the identity of nature [between reason and property to be proved], the absence [of the property to be proved] in the absence of that [reason] is also thereby established. Likewise, when [negative concomitance] is established, positive concomitance is also established. And the application of negative concomitance for the purpose of making known the restriction that the absence of the reason [should be known] only in the absence of that [property to be proved] — and not elsewhere, in the contrary instance (<s>vipakṣa</s>) or in contradictory [cases] — is also not appropriate, since what is other [than the <s>sādhya</s>] and what is contradictory [to it] are also instances of the contrary (<s>vipakṣa</s>).

body.text: (2.7) kathamidam avagamyate sadavaśyaṃ naśvarasvabhāvamiti yena anvayavyatirekasambhava iti cet / vināśahetvayogāt / svabhāvata eva bhāvā naśvarāḥ naiṣāṃ svahetubhyo niṣpatrānāmanyato vināśotpattiḥ / tasyāsāmarthyāt / na hi vināśaheturbhāvasya svabhāvameva karoti tasya svahetubhyo nirvṛtteḥ / nāpi bhāvāntarameva, bhāvāntarakaraṇe bhāvasya tadavasthatvāt tathopalabdhyādiprasaṅgaḥ / nāpi svabhāvāntaramasyāvaraṇam tadavasthe tasminnāvaraṇāyogāt / nāpi vināśahetunā bhāvābhāvaḥ kriyate / abhāvasya vidhinānyatayopagame vyatirekāvyatireka vikalpānatikramāt / bhāvapratiṣedhakaraṇe na tasya kiñcidbhavati na bhavatyeva kevalamiti / evaṃ ca kartā na bhavatītyakarturahetutvamiti na vināśahetuḥ kaścit /
body.translated_text: (2.7) [Objection:] How is it known that what exists is necessarily of a perishable nature, such that positive and negative concomitance (<s>anvaya-vyatireka</s>) are possible? — [Reply:] Because there is no [separate] cause of destruction. Entities are perishable by their very nature; for those that have arisen from their own causes, there is no arising of destruction from something else — because [any such external cause] lacks the capacity [to do so]. For a cause of destruction does not produce the very nature of an entity, since that is already accomplished by its own causes. Nor does it merely produce another entity, because if it produces another entity while the [original] entity remains unchanged, there would be the absurd consequence of perceiving it as still in the same state. Nor does another nature of the entity conceal it, because concealment is impossible for what remains in the same state. Nor does a cause of destruction bring about the non-existence of the entity. For if non-existence (<s>abhāva</s>) is admitted as a positive reality different [from the entity], one cannot escape the alternatives of either the exclusion departing or not departing. And if [the cause of destruction] produces the negation of the entity, then nothing at all belongs to it — it simply does not exist. And thus there is no agent, and since what has no agent has no cause, there is no cause of destruction whatsoever.

body.text: (2.8) vaiyarthyācca / yadi svabhāvato naśvaraḥ svātmanyanavasthāyī bhāvaḥ tasya na kiñcinnāśakāraṇaiḥ / tatsvabhāvatayaiva svayaṃ nāśāt / yo hi yatsvabhāvaḥ sa svahetoreva utpadyamānaḥ tādṛśo bhavati, na punastadbhāve hetvantaramapekṣate / prakāśadravoṣṇakaṭhinadravyādivat / na hi prakāśādayastadātmāna utpannāḥ punaḥ prakāśādibhāve hetvantaramapekṣante / tadātmanastādātmyābhāve nairātmyaprasaṅgāt / tadvadasthitidharmā cet svabhāvato bhāvo niṣpanno na punastadātmatāyāṃ hetvantaramapekṣate /
body.translated_text: (2.8) And because [a separate cause of destruction would be] purposeless. If an entity is perishable by nature, not abiding in its own self, then causes of destruction have no role for it — because it perishes by itself, by its very nature. For whatever has a given nature arises as such from its own cause alone, and does not require another cause for being of that nature — like luminous, liquid, hot, or hard substances and the like. For luminosity and the like, having arisen as of that nature, do not require another cause for being luminous and so forth — because if they lacked that nature despite being of that nature, there would be the absurd consequence of their having no [real] self (<s>nairātmya</s>). Likewise, if an entity arises by nature endowed with the property of permanence, once produced it does not require another cause for being of that nature.

body.text: (2.9) bījādivadanekānta iti cet / syādetad bījādayo 'ṅkurādijananasvabhāvā / api salilādihetvantarāpekṣaṇāt na kevalā janayanti / tadvad bhāvo 'pi vināśe syādīt / na / tasvabhāvasya jananādajanakasya cātatsvabhāvatvāt / ata eva tayoravasthayorvastubhedo niśceyaḥ / bhāvānāṃ svabhāvānyathātvābhāvāt tatsvabhāvasya paścādiva prāgāpi jananaprasaṅgāt /
body.translated_text: (2.9) [Objection:] Like seeds and the like, there is inconclusiveness (<s>anekānta</s>). It might be argued: seeds and the like have the nature of generating sprouts and the like, yet because they depend on other causes such as water, they do not generate [sprouts] by themselves alone. Likewise, an entity too might [require an additional cause] for its destruction. — [Reply:] No. Because [destruction] belongs to the nature of that which has been produced, and that which has not been produced does not have that nature. For this very reason, a real difference between those two states must be ascertained. Since there is no alteration of the nature of entities, there would be the absurd consequence that their nature of generating [sprouts] would apply even before [the seed matures], just as it applies after.

body.text: tasmādyo 'ntyo 'vasthāviśeṣaḥ sa evāṅkurajananasvabhāvaḥ / pūrvabhāvinastu avasthāviśeṣā aṅkurakāraṇasya kāraṇāni iti nānekāntaḥ / kṣaṇikeṣu bhāveṣu aparāparotpatteraikyābhāvāt /
body.translated_text: Therefore, only the final particular state [of the seed] has the nature of generating the sprout. The earlier particular states are causes of the cause of the sprout — thus there is no inconclusiveness (<s>anekānta</s>). In momentary (<s>kṣaṇika</s>) entities, since there is no identity due to the successive arising [of different states],

body.text: (2.10) yadi te 'ntyāḥ samarthāḥ kiṃ na janayanti pratyekamiti / janayantyeva nātrānyathābhāvaḥ svabhāsyāvaiparītyāt / nanu teṣu sahakāriṣu samarthasvabhāveṣu ko 'parasyopayogaḥ? na vai bhāvānāṃ kācit prekṣāpūrvakāritā yataḥ ayamasmāsvanyatamo 'pi samarthaḥ kimasmābhiḥ kartavyam ityālocyāpare nivarteran / te nirabhiprāyavyāpārā eva svahetupariṇāmopanidhidharmāṇonopālambhamarhanti, tatprakṛteḥ / te samarthāḥ kiṃ nāparāparaṃ janayantīti cet / na, tatraiva sāmarthyāt tasyaivaikasya janane samarthā nānyasyeti nāparāparajananam /
body.translated_text: (2.10) [Objection:] If those final [states] are capable, why does not each one produce [the sprout] individually? — [Reply:] They do indeed produce it; there is no difference here, since there is no reversal of their own nature. [Objection:] But if those cooperating conditions are of a capable nature, what is the use of the others? — [Reply:] Entities do not act with deliberation, such that [they would think] 'this particular one among us is also capable — what need is there for us?' and the others would withdraw. They, having purposeless activity, being subject to the conditions of their own causes' transformation, are not to be criticized — because it is their nature. [Objection:] If they are capable, why do they not generate [effects] successively? — [Reply:] No, because their capacity is directed only there — they are capable of generating only that one [effect], not another; therefore there is no successive generation.

body.text: (2.11) bhinnasvabhāvebhyaścakṣurādibhyaḥ sahakāribhya ekakāryotpattau na kāraṇabhedāt kāryabhedaḥ syāditi cet / na / yathāsvaṃ svabhāvabhedena tadviśeṣopayogastadupayogaiḥ kāryasvabhāvaviśeṣāsaṅkarāt / yathā mṛtpiṇḍakulālasūtrā dibhyo bhavato ghaṭasya mṛtpiṇḍādamṛtsvabhāvebhyo vṛkṣādibhyo bhinnaḥ svabhāvaḥ kulālāttasyaiva mṛdātmanaḥ sataḥ saṃsthāviśeṣātmatayā tadanyebhyo bhinnaḥ sūtrāttasyaiva mṛtsaṃsthāna viśeṣātmanaḥ cakrādervibhaktaḥ svabhāvo bhavati / tadevaṃ na kulālānmṛtsvabhāvatāḥ, na mṛdaḥ saṃsthānaviśeṣaḥ / na ca tayoḥ śāktiviśeṣaviṣayabhede 'pi tajjanitaviśeṣabhedasya kāryasya svabhāvena bhedaḥ mṛtsaṃsthānayoraparasparātmatayā saṃsthānamṛdrūpābhyāṃ tayorapratibhāsanaprasaṅgāt /
body.translated_text: (2.11) [Objection:] When a single effect arises from cooperating conditions of different natures — such as the eye and the like — there should be no difference in the effect due to the difference in causes. — [Reply:] No. Each [cause], by its own particular nature, contributes its own specific utility; and because the specific natures of the effects are not confused, owing to those respective utilities. Just as from a lump of clay, a potter, a cord, and the like, a pot comes into being: from non-clay-natured [causes] such as trees and the like, [the pot's] nature is distinct; from the potter, to that which is already of clay-nature, [there comes] distinction from others through a specific configuration; from the cord, to that which is already of clay-and-specific-configuration nature, [there comes] a nature distinct from the wheel and the like. Thus, clay-nature does not come from the potter, nor does specific configuration come from the clay. And although there is a difference in the domain of their respective powers, there is no [real] difference by nature in the effect as a distinctly produced particular — because, since clay and configuration are not each other's nature, there would be the absurd consequence of configuration and clay-form not appearing respectively [as what they are].

body.text: (2.12) anyadeva saṃsthānaṃ guṇo mṛddravyāt tena bhinnasvabhāvaḥ kulālamṛtpiṇḍayorupayogaviśeṣa iti cet / uktamatra / api ca yadi saṃsthānaṃ bhinnaṃ mṛdaḥ kulālaḥ kiṃ na pṛthakkaroti? guṇasya dravyaparatantratvāt sa kathaṃ pṛthak kriyeta? tatsaṃsthānādhārātmakaṃ yadi svabhāvenaiva tad dravyam, tatsaṃsthānaṃ vā tadādheyātmakaṃ, tadā kimiti kulālavyāpāramapekṣate iti cet / na / tataḥ parasparasambandhayogyatāpratilambhāt / anyathā mṛtpiṇḍasya svabhāvata eva tathāvidhasaṃsthānasambandhayogyatve vastuna eva prāgapi yogyatālakṣaṇā dharmatāstīti saṃsthānaviśeṣeṇa sambandhaḥ syāditi / evaṃ tarthi sā yogyatā mṛddravyasya kulālād bhavatīti nānayoḥ svabhāvabhedaḥ / bhedehi prāgvat prasajyeta / asti tāvadekasvabhāvatve 'pi ekasyānekapratyayopādheyaviśeṣateti kiṃ mṛtsaṃsthānayoḥ ekasvabhāvatvasādhanāya atinirbandhena /
body.translated_text: (2.12) [Objection:] Configuration (<s>saṃsthāna</s>) is indeed a quality (<s>guṇa</s>) different from the clay substance (<s>mṛd-dravya</s>), and being of a different nature from it, the difference in utility between the potter's [product] and the clay lump [is explained]. — [Reply:] This has already been addressed. Moreover, if configuration is different from clay, why does the potter not separate them? [Objection:] Since a quality depends on its substance, how could it be separated? If the substance is by its own nature the substratum of that configuration, or if that configuration is by nature what is superimposed upon the substratum, then why does it require the potter's activity? — [Reply:] No, because the fitness for mutual relation (<s>yogyatā</s>) is obtained from that [potter's activity]. Otherwise, if the clay lump had by its very nature the fitness for relation with such a configuration, then the thing would already possess a fitness-characterized property even before [the potter's work], and there would be relation with the particular configuration [without the potter]. If so, then that fitness of the clay substance comes from the potter, and so there is no difference of nature between the two. For if there were a difference, the same fault as before would follow. Indeed, even in something of a single nature, there can be particularization superimposed by multiple conditions — so why the excessive insistence on proving the single-naturedness of clay and configuration?

body.text: (2.13) tena sahakāriṇaḥ pratyayā naikopayogaviṣayāḥ kāryasyaikasvabhāvatve 'pi vastuta iti yatheha kāraṇabhedo bhinnaviśeṣopayogāt naikakāryaḥ, tathā cakṣurādibhyo vijñānotpattau utreyaḥ / tathā hi - samanantarapratyayādvijñānāccakṣurvijñānasya upalambhātmatā tasyaivopalambhātmanaḥ sataścakṣurindriyādrūpagrahaṇayogyatāpratiniyamaḥ viṣayāttattulyarūpateti abhinnatve 'pi vastutaḥ kāryasya kāraṇānāṃ bhinnebhyaḥ svabhāvebhyo bhinnā eva viśeṣā bhvantīti na kāraṇabhede 'pi abhedastatkāryaviśeṣasya / ta evaite kāraṇaśaktibhedā yathāsvaṃ prativiśiṣṭakāryajanane 'vyavadheyaśaktitayā pratyupasthitāḥ kṣaṇikatvātsāmagrīkāryasya svabhāvasthityāśrayaityucyante / tathāhi tattebhyaḥ samastebhyaḥ upalambhātmakaṃ rūpagrahaṇaṃ pratiniyataṃ viṣayarūpaṃ ceti prativiśiṣṭasvabhāvamekameva jātam /
body.translated_text: (2.13) Therefore, the auxiliary conditions (<s>sahakāri-pratyaya</s>) are not of single utility, even though the effect is of a single nature in reality. Just as here the difference among causes does not produce a single effect, due to their utility for different particularizations, so too in the arising of consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>) from the eye and other [sense faculties]. For: from the immediately preceding condition (<s>samanantara-pratyaya</s>), i.e., from [the preceding] consciousness, comes the perceptive nature (<s>upalambhātmatā</s>) of eye-consciousness; of that very perceptive [consciousness] which exists, from the eye faculty (<s>cakṣur-indriya</s>) comes the determinate fitness for grasping form; from the object comes its conformity to the form of that [object]. Thus, even when the effect is undifferentiated in reality, from the different natures of the different causes there arise different particularizations indeed. So there is no non-difference of the effect's particularization even when there is difference among causes. These very differences of causal powers, present as powers whose capacity is unimpeded in generating their respective particular effects, are said to be the basis of the natural stability of the aggregate's effect — because of momentariness (<s>kṣaṇikatva</s>). For from all those [causes] together, there arises a single thing of particularized nature: perception that is of the nature of apprehension, grasping of form that is determinate, and the form of the object.

body.text: (2.14) apratirodhaśaktikeṣu anantarakāryeṣu anādheyaviśeṣeṇu kṣaṇikeṣu pratyayeṣu parasparaṃ kaḥ sahakārārthaḥ? na vai sarvatrātiśayotpādanaṃ sahakriyā kā tarhi? ekārthakaraṇaṃ yad bahūnāmapi / yathāntyasya kāraṇakalāpasya / tadeva mukhyaṃ sahakāritvaṃ sahakāriṇāṃ, tasyaivāntyasya kāraṇatvāt / tatra ca kṣaṇe ekasya svabhāvasyāvivekād viśeṣasya kartumaśakyatvāt, svabhāvāntarotpattilakṣaṇatvād viśeṣotpatteḥ / bhāvāntarajanane 'ntyatvameva hīyeta / tataśca na sākṣātkāraṇaṃ syāt / tasmānna kāraṇasya sahakāribhyo viśeṣasyotpattiḥ / te samarthā eva svabhāvato 'ntyāḥ pratyayāḥ saha jāyante kṣaṇikā yeṣāṃ prākpaścātpṛthagbhāvo nāsti, yebhyaścānantarameva kāryamutpadyate / tatra ekārthakriyaiva sahakāritvam /
body.translated_text: (2.14) When the conditions are momentary (<s>kṣaṇika</s>), with unimpeded power, with immediate effects that have no further particularization to be imposed — what is the purpose of mutual cooperation? Cooperation (<s>sahakriyā</s>) is certainly not the production of a surplus everywhere — then what is it? It is the working toward a single purpose (<s>ekārthakaraṇa</s>) by many [causes]. As in the case of the final causal aggregate. That alone is the primary cooperation of the cooperating [causes], since only that final [aggregate] is the cause. And therein, in a single moment, since a single nature cannot be differentiated, particularization cannot be produced — for the arising of particularization has the character of the arising of a different nature. If [the cause] were to generate a different entity, its finality would be lost. And then it would not be a direct cause. Therefore, the particularization of the effect does not arise from the cooperating [causes] of the cause. Those final conditions (<s>pratyaya</s>), which are capable by their own nature, arise together — being momentary, they have no separate prior or subsequent existence; and from them the effect arises immediately after. Therein, cooperation is nothing but the working toward a single result.

body.text: (2.15) samarthaḥ kuto jāyata iti cet / svakāraṇebhyaḥ / tāni enamaparasannidhāna evaṃ kiṃ janayanti? kadācidanyathāpi syuḥ tataścaiko 'pi kvacit janayed iti cet / aparāpara pratyayayogena pratikṣaṇaṃ bhinnaśaktayaḥ saṃskārāḥ santanvanto yadyapi kutaścitsāmyātsarūpāḥ pratīyante tathāpi bhitra evaiṣāṃ svabhāvaḥ / tena kiñcideva kasyacit kāraṇam /
body.translated_text: (2.15) [Objection:] From what does the capable [cause] arise? — From its own causes. — Do those causes generate it only in the absence of other [conditions]? [Objection:] Sometimes they might be otherwise, and so even a single one might somewhere generate [the effect]. — [Reply:] The dispositional impressions (<s>saṃskāras</s>), which continue with powers differing at each moment through the connection with ever-different conditions, though they appear similar due to some commonality, nonetheless have a distinct nature. Therefore, only a specific thing is the cause of a specific [effect].

body.text: tatra yo 'vyavadhanādideśo rūpendriyādikalāpaḥ sa vijñānajanane samartho hetuḥ / yasteṣāṃ parasparopasarpaṇādyāśrayaḥ pratyayaviśeṣaḥ sa taddhetujanane samarthaḥ teṣāṃ ca na pūrvaṃ na paścātra pṛthagbhāva iti samarthānapi pūrvāparapṛthagbhāvbhāvino doṣā nopalīyante / tena yasteṣāṃ parasparopasarpaṇādihetuḥ sa samarthasya heturiti tatra na kadācidanyathābhāvaḥ /
body.translated_text: There, the aggregate of <s>rūpa</s> (form), sense-faculty (<s>indriya</s>), and the like that is in a position of non-obstruction etc. is the competent cause (<s>hetu</s>) for the production of consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>). The particular condition (<s>pratyayaviśeṣa</s>) that is the basis of their mutual approach and the like is competent for the production of that [particular] cause. And since these do not have separate existence before or after [each other], the defects [alleged against momentary causes] do not attach even to competent [causes] existing in prior and posterior separate states. Therefore, whatever is the cause of their mutual approach etc. is the cause of the competent [cause], and there is never any change in that [causal relation].

body.text: (2.16) anena nyāyena sarvatra hetuphalabhāvapratiniyamo draṣṭavyaḥ pratikṣaṇamanyānyasvabhāvabhedānvayinīṣu śaktiṣu, na tu sthiraikasvabhāveṣu bhāveṣu svabhāvasyānyathātvāsaṃbhavāt / samarthāsamarthasvabhāvayoḥ kriyākriyānupapatteḥ / anyasahitaḥ karoti na kevala iti cet / kiṃ kevalasya kāryajanane 'samarthaḥ svabhāvaḥ? samartha iti cet / kiṃ na karoti? akurvan kathaṃ samarthaḥ? kuvindādayaḥ paṭādikriyāyāṃ samarthā api na sarvatra kurvantīti cet / krīḍanaśīlo devānāṃ priyaḥ sukhaidhitaḥ kṛtamapi punaḥ punaḥ kārayati, tathāhi bījādivad ityanena nirloṭhitameva / tasmātsvabhāvasyānyathātvāsambhavāt taddharmaṇaḥ tathābhāvaḥ antyāvasthāvadanivāryaḥ /
body.translated_text: (2.16) By this principle, the invariable determination of the cause-effect relation is to be seen everywhere among capacities (<s>śakti</s>) that are linked to differences of nature changing at every moment, but not in entities of stable, single nature—because the nature cannot become otherwise. For [there would be] the impossibility of action and non-action for natures that are competent and incompetent [respectively]. [Objection:] It acts when conjoined with others, not alone. [Reply:] Is its nature then incompetent for producing the effect by itself? [Objection:] It is competent. [Reply:] Then why does it not act? Not acting, how is it competent? [Objection:] Weavers and the like, though competent in the production of cloth and the like, do not produce everywhere. [Reply:] One who is playful by disposition, dear to the gods, nourished by happiness, causes things to be made again and again even when already made—as has been thoroughly examined by the [analogy of] "like a seed and so forth." Therefore, since the nature cannot become otherwise, its property of being in such a state is unavoidable, as in the final stage.

body.text: antyāvasthāyāṃ prāgasamarthasya sāmarthyotpattau tasya sāmarthyasya tatsvabhāvatve 'pūrvotpattirevasā / atatsvabhāvatve saḥ akāraka eva sāmarthyākhyātpadārthāntarāt kāryotpattyabhyupagamāt /
body.translated_text: If in the final stage competence arises for what was previously incompetent, and if that competence is of its nature, then this is simply a new arising. If it is not of its nature, then that [entity] is indeed a non-agent, since the production of the effect would have to be accepted from another thing called "competence."

body.text: (2.17) api ca yo 'sau sakaleṣu sahakāriṣu karoti sa tadaiva kasmāt karoti / ? kurvan dṛṣṭastena karotīti brūmaḥ / aho mahāsāmarthyaṃ mahāprabhāvasya darśanaṃ yasmādatatsvabhāvān api bhāvān svabhāvamātreṇa nānāprakāreṣu vyāpāreṣu niyuṅkte / yadi nāma kiñcit kathañcidatrabhavato darśanaviṣayatām atikrāmet, hanta aprasavadharmakamapetasantānaṃ syaditīyaṃ cintā cittaṃ dunoti /
body.translated_text: (2.17) Moreover, that which acts when all cooperative conditions (<s>sahakārin</s>) are present—why does it act only then? [Reply:] We say it acts because it is observed to act. Oh, what great power! What a magnificent vision of the greatly powerful one, that by mere nature it engages things that are not of its own nature in various activities! If anything were to somehow escape the scope of the honored one's perception, alas, it would be without the capacity for production, devoid of a continuum—this worry torments the mind.

body.text: na vai vayam atatsvabhāvānāṃ bhāvānām asmaddarśanavaśāt kāryakriyāṃ brūmaḥ kintu svabhāvenaiva te kāryakāraṇadharmāḥ, tān paśyantaḥ kevalaṃ jānīmahe te ete kārakasvabhāvā iti /
body.translated_text: We do not assert the efficient action (<s>kāryakriyā</s>) of entities that are not of their own nature merely on the basis of our observation. Rather, by their very nature they possess cause-and-effect properties; seeing them, we merely know: "these are of the nature of agents (<s>kāraka</s>)."

body.text: (2.18) satyam idamapyasti, svabhāvasteṣāṃ kāryakriyādharmā tena samastapratyayānāmakṛtvā kāryaṃ nopekṣāpattiriti / so 'kṣepakriyādharmā svabhāvaḥ kiṃ teṣāṃ tadaivāntyāvasthāyāmutpanna āhosvit prāgapyāsīt? āsīt, apracyutā nutpatrasthiraikasvabhāvānā kadācit kasyacitsvabhāvasyābhāvavirodhāt / tatkimidānīṃ mātā ca vandhyā ca asti? ko vāsya bhāṣitasyārthaḥ- akṣepakriyāsvabhāvaḥ kāryaṃ ca na karotīti /
body.translated_text: (2.18) Indeed this too is true: their nature possesses the property of efficient action; therefore, without [the gathering of] all conditions, the effect does not arise, and there is no charge of neglect. But this nature possessing the property of gathering-action—did it arise in them only at that time, in the final stage, or did it exist before as well? [Reply:] It existed [before], since for entities of stable, single, and unchanging nature, the non-existence of any nature at any time is contradictory. Then is this [entity] both a mother and barren? Or what is the meaning of this statement—"its nature possesses the property of gathering-action, yet it does not produce the effect"?

body.text: (2.19) sahitaḥ svakāryajananasvabhāvaḥ na kevala iti cet / anyastarhi kevalo 'nyaśca sahitaḥ svabhāvabhedāt / svabhāvabheda eva hi bhāvabhedasya lakṣaṇam / na hi sa sāhitye 'pi pararūpeṇa kartā syāt / svarūpaṃ ca tasya prāgapi tadeveti kathaṃ kadacit kriyāvirāmaḥ /
body.translated_text: (2.19) [Objection:] Its nature of producing its own effect is [operative only] when conjoined, not alone. [Reply:] Then the one that is alone is different from the one that is conjoined, due to the difference in nature. For a difference of nature is indeed the defining mark of a difference of entity. For it would not be an agent through another's form even when conjoined. And since its own form was the same even before, how is there ever a cessation of activity?

body.text: yasyāpi bhāvah kṣaṇikaḥ tasyāpi kasmāt kevalo na karoti? yadi bhavet kuryādeva / kathaṃ na bhavati? kṣaṇikatvāt / uktaṃ yādṛśasya kriyā / sa kathamekakṣaṇabhāvī anyathā bhavet? yaśca bhavati sa eva na bhavatīti nāyaṃ prasaṅgaḥ kārakākārakayoḥ svabhāvataddhetvorvirodhāt /
body.translated_text: [Objection:] Even for one whose entity is momentary (<s>kṣaṇika</s>), why does it not act when alone? [Reply:] If it were [to exist alone], it would indeed act. [Objection:] How does it not exist [alone]? [Reply:] Because of momentariness (<s>kṣaṇikatva</s>). It has been stated what kind [of entity's] action [this is]. How could that which exists for only one moment become otherwise? And the objection—"the very one that exists [as agent] also does not exist [as agent]"—does not apply, because there is a contradiction between the natures and their causes for agents and non-agents.

body.text: (2.20) yo 'pi manyate- akṣepakriyādharmaiva sa tasya svabhāvaḥ, na sa sāhityamapekṣate, kāryaṃ tu pratyayāntarāpekṣamiti sahitebhya eva jāyate na kevalebhya iti, tasyāpi kathaṃ- sa bhāvaḥ kevalo 'pi karotyeva? kāryaṃ ca tasmātrotpadyate iti tadavastho virodhaḥ / na kevalaḥ karotyeveti cet / kathamidānīmakṣepakriyāsvabhāvaḥ / nanu etadeva paridīpitaṃ bhavati, karotyeveti / kāryaṃ cāyaṃ kevalo 'pi samarthaḥ san paramapekṣamāṇaṃ kathamupekṣeta? paramanādṛtyaitat prasahya kuryāt / evaṃ hi anenātmanaḥ sāmarthyaṃ darśitaṃ bhavati / kāryaṃ paramapekṣata iti tataḥ kevalād anutpattimasya kathayasi sa kevalo 'pi samarthasvabhāva iti tataḥ utpattiṃ brūṣe, ete ca kathamevatraṃ syātām? tadayamīrṣyāśalyavitudyamānamarmā viklavaṃ vikrośatītyupekṣāmevārhati / tasmādidamekārthakriyālakṣaṇaṃ sahakāritvaṃ kṣaṇikānāmeva bhāvānām / na tu akṣaṇikānāṃ yeṣāṃ pṛthagapi bhāvaḥ sambhavati pṛthak kāryakaraṇasambhavena sahakāritvaniyamāyogāt /
body.translated_text: (2.20) As for one who thinks: 'The property of initiating activity (<s>akṣepakriyā</s>) alone is its nature; it does not depend on conjunction [with other causes], but the effect depends on other conditions — hence it arises only from [causes] in conjunction, not from [causes] individually' — for him too, [we ask:] how is it that the entity, even individually, does indeed act? And the effect arises from it — [thus] the same contradiction remains. [Objection:] It does not act individually. — [Reply:] Then how is it of the nature of initiating activity? [Objection:] Surely, this is precisely what is indicated — that 'it does indeed act.' — [Reply:] But if this [entity], being individually capable, [has an effect that] depends on another — how could it disregard [the effect]? Disregarding the other [conditions], it should forcibly produce [the effect]. For thus its own capacity would be demonstrated. You say that the effect depends on another, and from this [argue for] its non-arising from [the cause] individually; [yet] you also say that it is individually of a capable nature, and from this [argue for] its arising — how can both of these be true? Therefore, this one, with his vital points pierced by the thorn of jealousy, is crying out helplessly, and deserves merely to be disregarded. Therefore, this cooperation (<s>sahakāritva</s>), defined as working toward a single causal efficacy (<s>ekārthakriyā</s>), belongs only to momentary (<s>kṣaṇika</s>) entities — not to non-momentary ones, for which separate existence is possible; since their separate capacity to produce effects makes the restriction of cooperation impossible.

body.text: (2.21) yatra tu santānopakāreṇa bhāvāḥ hetutāṃ pratipadyante, yathā taṇḍulabījādibhya odanāṅkurādijanmani dahanodakapṛthivyādayaḥ, tatra santānāśrayeṇa viśeṣotpādanaṃ pratyayānāṃ sahakriyocyate na dravyāśrayeṇa, kṣaṇike dravye viśeṣasyānutpatteḥ / nahi taṇḍulādīnāṃ viśeṣānutpattau dahanādibhāve 'pi odanajanma syāt / tathā prabhāsvarādapavarakaṃ praviṣṭasya yadīndriyaṃ svopakāribhyo 'tiśayaṃ krameṇa na pratipadyeta tadā prāgivārthapratilpattiṃ naiva janayet /
body.translated_text: (2.21) But where entities become causes through the aid of a continuum (<s>santāna</s>) — as when fire, water, earth, and the like [contribute to] the production of cooked rice, sprouts, and so forth from rice grains, seeds, and the like — there, the production of particularization by the conditions is called cooperation (<s>sahakriyā</s>) based on the continuum, not based on a [single] substance, because no particularization arises in a momentary substance. For if no particularization arises in the rice grains and the like, then even in the presence of fire and other [conditions], cooked rice would not be produced. Likewise, if the sense faculty of one who has entered a dark chamber from a bright [space] did not gradually acquire enhancement from its beneficial [conditions], then it would never produce perception of an object, just as before [entering].

body.text: akṣepakāriṣu indriyādiṣu na viśeṣotpattiḥ parasparataḥ sambhavati / tatra yathāsvaṃ pratyayaiḥ parasparopasarpaṇādyāśrayairye yogyadeśādyavasthā jātāste saha svabhāvaniṣpattyā jñānahetutāṃ pratipadyante ityekārthakriyaiva sahakāritvam /
body.translated_text: Among causes that initiate [activity], such as the sense faculties and the like, no particularization arises from one another. There, through their respective conditions — [conditions] whose basis is mutual proximity and the like — those that have attained the state of fitness in appropriate locations and the like, together with the accomplishment of their [respective] natures, become causes of cognition (<s>jñāna</s>). Thus, cooperation is nothing but working toward a single purpose (<s>ekārthakriyā</s>).

body.text: (2.22) yatra tu viśeṣamutpādayantaḥ sahakāriṇaḥ pratyayāḥ tatra hetusantānaḥ pratyayāntarāṇyapekṣata iti tataḥ svabhāvāntarasya pratilambhaḥ / tatra svarasataḥ hetupratyayānāṃ pūrvopanipātakṣaṇānāṃ nivṛttau tebhya eva viśiṣṭakṣaṇotpattirevaṃ krameṇa yāvadatyantātiśayavato 'ntyakāraṇakalāpāt kāryotpattiḥ /
body.translated_text: (2.22) But where cooperating conditions (<s>sahakāri-pratyaya</s>) produce particularization, there the causal continuum depends on other conditions, and from that [dependence] there is the obtaining of a different nature. There, when the preceding moments of the cause and conditions naturally cease, from those very [causes] a particularized moment arises; and thus, progressively, until from the final causal aggregate possessing the utmost enhancement, the effect arises.

body.text: (2.23) sahakāriṇaḥ samutpatraviśeṣātkāraṇātkāryotpattau tasyaiva viśeṣasyotpattirna syāt / aviśiṣṭādviśeṣotpattau kāryasyāpi syāt / tataśca parasparaviśeṣotpādānapekṣiṇa eva sahakāriṇaḥ kāryaṃ kurvīran / tenākṣaṇikānāmapi sahakārisāpekṣāṇāṃ kāraṇatā syāt / apekṣaṇīyebhyaḥ svabhāvātiśayotpattiśca na syāt /
body.translated_text: (2.23) If the effect arises from a cause that is a particularized cooperating [condition], then that very particularization would not arise [if the cause is already particularized]. If particularization arises from what is unparticularized, then [it] would also [arise] for the effect [without any cause]. And then the cooperating conditions, without depending on mutual particularization, would produce the effect. Therefore, even non-momentary entities, when dependent on cooperating conditions, would have causal capacity. And no arising of an enhanced nature from those upon which [the entity] depends would occur.

body.text: atha sahakāriṇā kāryotpādānuguṇaviśeṣajananāya kṛtaviśeṣa evopattiṣṭheta / evaṃ satyanavasthā syāt / na ca sahakāriṇaḥ parasparakāryotpādānuguṇaviśeṣotpādane nityaṃ yogyāvasthāḥ, yena nityānuṣakta eṣāṃ viśeṣaḥ syāt / tadupāyāpāyayoḥ kāryasyotpattyanutpattidarśanāt / tenādyo viśeṣaḥ sahakāribhyo nirupakārasya notpadyata iti cet / nāsmākaṃ punaḥ punarabhidhāne 'pi kaścidudvego bhavati yadyevamapi lokasya nyāyapratītirbhavati / hanta tarhi ucyatām / na viśeṣotpādanāt sahakāriṇāṃ sahakāritvaṃ paramārthataḥ sambhavati / yataḥ tadabhāvādviśeṣe kartavye sahakāritāvirahaḥ syāt /
body.translated_text: [Objection:] Then the [cause], having been particularized by the cooperating condition for the purpose of producing a particularization conducive to producing the effect, would only then [function as cause]. — [Reply:] If so, there would be an infinite regress (<s>anavasthā</s>). And the cooperating conditions are not eternally in a state of fitness for producing particularization conducive to producing each other's effects, such that their particularization would be permanently attached to them — because the arising and non-arising of the effect is observed in accordance with the availability and non-availability of those [conditions]. [Objection:] Then the initial particularization does not arise for one who is unaided by cooperating conditions. — [Reply:] We are not at all distressed even by repeated statements [of this objection], if thereby the common understanding of the world is [properly] established. Very well then, let it be stated: the cooperation of cooperating conditions is not ultimately possible through the production of particularization — because, in its absence, when particularization needs to be produced, there would be an absence of cooperating [capacity].

body.text: (2.24) atha kathamekārthakriyāpi bhavet sāpi na bhavet parasparato viśeṣarahitānām / atha bhavet, pṛthagapi sā bhavet / tathāca, tasmād viśeṣād bhavanaśīlaṃ kāryamapi kevalāt syāditi cet / atroktamuttaraṃ pratikṣaṇamaparāparaiḥ pratyayaiḥ yathā bhāvasantāne viśeṣasyotpattiḥ, yogyadeśatādyavasthāviśeṣāḥ kāryakaraṇaśīlāḥ, teṣāṃ ca yata utpattiḥ, pratyekaṃ ca sāmarthye 'pi kevalānāmakriyā, kartṛviśeṣasya pṛthagekaikasya bhāvasyābhāvāt / kāryadvaividhyaṃ ca sahakāribhiḥ akṣepakārindriyavijñānavacca kāryakāraṇayoḥ svabhāvabhedāditi sarvamuktam /
body.translated_text: [Objection:] Now, how could even a single causal efficacy (<s>arthakriyā</s>) occur [from multiple causes that are] mutually undifferentiated? And if it could occur, it would occur from each one individually as well. And thus, the effect, which is of the nature to arise from that particular differentiation, would also arise from [each cause] alone. — [Reply:] The answer to this has already been stated: how at each moment, through ever-different conditions, differentiation arises in the causal series (<s>bhāvasantāna</s>); how the particular states of suitable location and the like are capable of producing effects; how those [particular states] arise from [their respective causes]; and how, even though each individually has capacity, those [causes] alone do not act [individually], because the particular agent — that is, each individual entity separately — does not exist [as such]. And the twofold nature of the effect in relation to cooperating causes — just as in the case of the sense faculty and consciousness that produce [their effects] by attraction (<s>ākṣepa</s>) — [arises] from the difference in the nature of cause and effect: all this has been stated.

body.text: (2.25) tatra sahakāribhyaḥ santānopakārāpekṣakāraṇakāryajanmani sahakāriṇāmādyo viśeṣaḥ sahakārikṛtaviśeṣajanmā na bhavati, anantarakāryavat, tataḥ ye viśeṣā jāyante te tajjanmānaḥ tatprakṛtitvāditi nānavasthā / tathā yadyakṣaṇiko 'pi bhāvaḥ kārya karoti, karotu nāma, sa yadi akṣepakartṛdharmā, tadā pṛthagbhāvasya sambhavātkevalo 'pi tathā syād ityuktam / atatsvabhāvastu tadāpyakāraka eva /
body.translated_text: There, in the production of an effect from a cause that depends on the assistance of the [causal] series by cooperating conditions — the first differentiation of the cooperating conditions is not one that is born from a differentiation produced by those cooperating conditions, just like the immediately subsequent effect. The differentiations that arise from those [cooperating conditions] are born from them and are of their nature — thus there is no infinite regress (<s>anavasthā</s>). Likewise, even if a non-momentary entity performs an effect — let it perform it — if it has the property of producing [effects] by attraction, then since a separate entity [of that kind] is possible, even a single one would act thus — this has been stated. But what is not of that nature is non-productive even then.

body.text: tasmādakṣaṇikānāṃ kāraṇānām ekārthakriyayā na kaścit sahakāritvaniyamaḥ / nāpi santatyopakāreṇeti na tasya kaścitsahakārīti kevalo 'pi kuryāt / prāyastu saṃghātasthāyī bhāvasantānaḥ sahakāripratyayairupajanitaviśeṣaḥ svakāryaṃ kurvan dṛṣṭo bījādivat / tatsthirahetuvādino hetoḥ pratyayāntarāpekṣakārakasya vyaktaṃ svabhāvāntarasyotpattiḥ / kārakasvabhāvasya prāgapi sattve 'kriyā na yujyate /
body.translated_text: Therefore, for non-momentary causes, there is no rule regarding cooperation through a single causal efficacy. Nor [is there such a rule] through assistance to the [causal] series — therefore, since there is no cooperating condition for it, [a non-momentary cause] would produce [the effect] even alone. But what is generally observed is a causal series persisting in an aggregate, with differentiation generated by cooperating conditions, producing its own effect — like seeds and the like. For the proponent of a permanent cause: when the cause that depends on other conditions for its productive capacity manifestly [undergoes] the arising of a different nature — if the productive nature already existed before, the absence of [productive] action [then] is untenable.

body.text: (2.26) tasmādyo yadātmā sa svasattāmātreṇa tādṛśo bhavati na bhūtvā tadbhāve parābhisaṃskāramapekṣata iti svabhāvato 'sthitidharmaṇo bhāvasya na kiñcitrāśakāraṇaiḥ / sthitidharmaṇo 'pi bhāvasya na nāśakāraṇaiḥ kiñcit svabhāvānyathātvasya kenacit kartumaśakyatvāt / tadanyathātvapratipattau sa tatsvabhāva eva na syāditi pūrva eva vikalpaḥ syāt / tatra ca prāgevoktaṃ dūṣaṇam /
body.translated_text: Therefore, whatever has a given nature becomes of that nature by its mere existence alone and does not depend on external conditioning (<s>parābhisaṃskāra</s>) for being of that nature — thus for an entity whose nature is not to persist (<s>asthitidharman</s>), there is nothing [to be accomplished] by causes of destruction. For an entity whose nature is to persist (<s>sthitidharman</s>) too, there is nothing [to be accomplished] by causes of destruction, because a change in its intrinsic nature (<s>svabhāvānyathātva</s>) cannot be brought about by anything. If [its nature were] apprehended as changed, then it would no longer be of that very nature — and this would be the very first alternative [already discussed]. And the refutation of that has already been stated.

body.text: yaśca parasmādanyathābhāvaḥ so 'paraḥ svabhāvaḥ yaścāparaḥ sa kathaṃ tasya syāt? svabhāvabhedo hi vastubhedalakṣaṇam / tathā ca yaḥ sthitidharmā jātaḥ na tasyānyathābhāvaḥ syāt / etena kaṭhinādīnāṃ tāmrādīnām agnyādeḥ dravatvādisvabhāvāntarotpattiḥ pratyuktā / tatrāpi pūrvakasya svarasanirodhitvādvināśe 'gnyāderupādānāccāpara eva dravādisvabhāvaḥ utpannaḥ /
body.translated_text: And the change of state arising from something external — that is a different nature; and how could what is different belong to it [the original entity]? For a difference in nature is the defining mark of a difference in real entities (<s>vastubheda</s>). And thus, for one that has arisen with the nature of persisting, there would be no change of state. By this, the arising of a different nature such as liquidity and the like in hard things like copper and the like [when acted upon] by fire and the like is refuted. For even there, the prior [entity] ceases by its own nature; and through the material cause (<s>upādāna</s>) of fire and the like, an altogether different entity of liquid and similar nature is produced.

body.text: (2.27) sa svayaṃ sthitidharmaiva svahetubhirjanitaḥ, vināśahetorasambhave 'vasthānāt / tasya parasmādvināśo bhavati iti / na ca vināśo nāmāparaḥ svabhāvaḥ, bhāvacyutireva vināśaḥ iti cet / nedaṃ vikalpadvayamatikrāmati - kiṃ nityo bhāva utānityaḥ / prāṅnityo bhūtvā paścādanityo bhavatīti ca bruvāṇo bhāvadvayaṃ cāha nityānityasvabhāvabhedam / prāktanasya nityābhimatasya svabhāvasya svayaṃ nāśaṃ bruvāṇaḥ sarvadaiva nāśamanāśaṃ ca prāheti pūrvasmin vināśaheturasamartha eva /
body.translated_text: [Objection:] It [the entity] itself has the nature of persisting, having been produced by its own causes, since it remains so long as there is no cause of destruction. Its destruction comes from something external. And destruction is not a different nature — destruction is merely the cessation of being (<s>bhāvacyuti</s>). — [Reply:] This does not transcend the twofold alternative: is the entity permanent or impermanent? One who says 'having been permanent first, it becomes impermanent afterwards' is speaking of two entities of different natures — one permanent and one impermanent. And one who says that the formerly admitted permanent nature itself undergoes destruction on its own is at all times asserting both destruction and non-destruction — thus, in the first [case], the cause of destruction is utterly powerless.

body.text: na prāṅnityo bhūtvā paścādanityaḥ bhavati, kiṃ tarhi, paścādapi nitya eva, ekasvabhāvatvāt / sa tarhi bhāvaḥ svabhāvena nāśamanāviśan kathaṃ naṣṭo nāma? tatsvabhāvavināśayoḥ aparaspararūpatvāt / tasmāt satyasya vināśe vināśasvabhāvena tena bhavitavyaṃ, tathāpi vināśaheturvyartha ityuktam / tena svabhāvato naścare 'naśvare vā bhāve na vināśahetorupayogaḥ /
body.translated_text: [Reply continued:] It is not the case that, having been permanent first, it becomes impermanent afterwards; rather, it remains permanent afterwards as well, because it has a single nature. If so, how can an entity that does not undergo destruction by its nature be called 'destroyed'? Because its nature and its destruction are not of each other's form. Therefore, if it is truly destroyed, it must be of a destructible nature — and even so, the cause of destruction is pointless, as has been stated. Thus, whether the entity is perishable or imperishable by nature, there is no use for a cause of destruction.

body.text: (2.28) tasmādvināśaṃ pratyanapekṣo bhāvastadbhāvaniyataḥ iti yaḥ san sa vināśī naśvaratāyā nivṛttau sattvanivṛtirityanvayavyatirekasiddhiḥ /
body.translated_text: (2.28) Therefore, an entity (<s>bhāva</s>) is not dependent on [anything else] for its destruction; it is determined [to perish] by the very fact of its existence. Thus, whatever exists is perishable — upon the cessation of perishability, there is cessation of existence. This is the establishment through positive and negative concomitance (<s>anvaya-vyatireka</s>).

body.text: svabhāvato naśvaratve 'pi kaścidatatsvabhāvo 'pi syāt / na hi sarvaḥ sarvasya svabhāva iti na tatribandhanānvayavyatirekāsiddhiriti cet / na, akṣaṇikatve 'vastutvaprasaṅgāt / śaktirhi bhāvalakṣaṇam / sarvaśaktivirahaḥ punarabhāvalakṣaṇam / na caivākṣaṇikasya kvacit kācit śaktirasti, kramayaugapadyābhyāṃ kāryakriyāśakti virahāt / itthaṃ ca yat sattat kṣaṇikameveti vyāptisiddhiḥ /
body.translated_text: [Objection:] Even if perishability is by nature, some entity might have a different nature. For not everything is the nature of everything — so the positive and negative concomitance bound to that is not established. — [Reply:] No, because non-momentariness would entail the consequence of non-entity-hood (<s>avastutvaprasaṅga</s>). For capacity (<s>śakti</s>) is the defining characteristic of an entity (<s>bhāva</s>). The complete absence of all capacity is the defining characteristic of a non-entity (<s>abhāva</s>). And a non-momentary thing has no capacity whatsoever, due to the absence of causal efficacy (<s>kārya-kriyā-śakti</s>) both in sequence and simultaneously. Thus, the pervasion (<s>vyāpti</s>) is established: whatever exists is momentary (<s>kṣaṇika</s>).

body.text: (3.1) arthāntare gamye kāryaṃ heturavyabhicārāt / kāryakāraṇabhāvena gamakatve sarvathā gamyagamakabhāvaḥ syāt, sarvathā janyajanakabhāvād iti cet / na / tadabhāve bhavatastadutpattiniyamābhāvāt / tasmāt kāryaṃ svabhāvairyāvadbhiravinābhāvi kāraṇe teṣāṃ hetuḥ / tatkāryatvaniyamāt / taireva ca dharmairye tairvinā na bhavanti / aṃśena janyajanakabhāvaprasaṅga iti cet / na, tajjanyaviśeṣagrahaṇe 'bhimatatvāt liṅga viśeṣopādhīnāṃ ca sāmānyānām / aviśiṣṭasāmānyavivakṣāyāṃ vyabhicāra iti gamakatvaṃ neṣyate /
body.translated_text: (3.1) When something different is to be inferred, the effect (<s>kārya</s>) is the logical reason (<s>hetu</s>), due to its non-deviation (<s>avyabhicāra</s>). [Objection:] If the inferability is through the cause-effect relation, there would be inferability in every respect — since the producer-produced relation holds in every respect. — [Reply:] No, because in the absence of that [specific cause], there is no invariable arising of that [specific effect] from yours [i.e., from whatever you propose]. Therefore, the effect, being inseparable from whatever natures [constitute] the cause, is the logical reason for those [natures] — due to the invariability of being their effect. And those properties without which they [the effects] do not exist — [Objection:] There would be the consequence of the producer-produced relation holding only partially. — [Reply:] No, because it is intended that the specific qualifiers and the universals that function as limiting conditions of the logical mark (<s>liṅga</s>) apprehend the specific product. When an unspecified universal is intended, there is deviation (<s>vyabhicāra</s>), so inferability is not accepted.

body.text: (3.2) kasyacitkadācitkutaścidbhāve 'pi sarvastādṛśastathāvidhajanmeti kuto 'vasitam, tathā ca nānvayavyatirekāviti cet / na, atadbhāvinastasya sakṛdapi tato 'bhāvāt / parasparāpekṣayā janyajanakasvabhāvalakṣaṇe kāryakāraṇe / tatra yadi dhūmo 'gnyādisāmagjyā anyato 'pi bhavettadā tasya tajjanyaḥ svabhāvo na bhavatīti sakṛdapi tato na bhavet / arthāntaravat / nāpi sāmagrī taṃ janayed atajjananasvabhāvatvāt / sāmagjyantaravat / na ca dhūmasya tadatajjanyaḥ svabhāvo yuktaḥ / ekasvabhāvatvāt / dhūmādhūmajananasvabhāvād bhavato dhūmādhūmasvabhāvaḥ syāt / kāryasvabhāvānāṃ kāraṇasvabhāvakṛtatvāt / akāraṇāpekṣaṇe cāhetukatvaprasaṅgāt / tasmādyo dhūmajananaḥ so 'gnyādisāmagrīviśeṣo yaḥ agnyādisāmagrīviśeṣeṇa janitaḥ sa eva dhūmo bhavatīti kāryakāraṇayorevaṃ svabhāvasya niyamāt tadvijātīyādutpattirna bhavati /
body.translated_text: (3.2) [Objection:] Even if something arises from something, somewhere, at some time — how is it ascertained that everything of that kind arises from something of that kind? And thus there would be no positive and negative concomitance (<s>anvaya-vyatireka</s>). — [Reply:] No, because that which does not have that nature never arises from that, even once. Cause and effect are characterized by the producer-produced nature in mutual dependence. If smoke were to arise from something other than the aggregate of fire and the like, then it would not have the nature of being produced by that [fire-aggregate], and so it would never arise from it — just like any other thing. Nor would the aggregate produce it, since it does not have the nature of producing that — just like any other aggregate. Nor is it reasonable for smoke to have both the nature of being produced by that and not produced by that — because of its single nature. From a thing whose nature is to produce both smoke and non-smoke, there would follow the nature of being both smoke and non-smoke — because the natures of effects are determined by the natures of causes. And if [one says effects] do not depend on causes, there would be the consequence of having no cause (<s>ahetuka</s>). Therefore, that which produces smoke is the specific aggregate of fire and the like, and that which is produced by the specific aggregate of fire and the like is smoke alone. Due to this invariability of nature between cause and effect, there is no arising from something of a different kind.

body.text: tadyādṛśaṃ kāryaṃ yādṛśāt kāraṇād dṛṣṭamekadā tattanna vyabhicarati / tena siddhe kāryakāraṇabhāve kāryasya kāraṇena vyāptiḥ siddhā bhavati /
body.translated_text: Whatever kind of effect has been observed from whatever kind of cause on even one occasion — that does not deviate. Therefore, once the cause-effect relation is established, the pervasion (<s>vyāpti</s>) of the effect by the cause is established.

body.text: (3.3) nanu vijātīyādapi kiñcid bhavad dṛṣṭaṃ tadyathā go mayādeḥ śālūkādiḥ / na vijātīyādutpattiḥ / tathāvidhameva hi tādṛśāmādinimittamiti na kāraṇabhedaḥ / prabandhena vṛttau tu śarād bhavati / asti ca gomayetarajanmanoḥ svabhāvabhedaḥ rūpasyābhede 'pi / na hi ākāratulyataiva bhāvānāṃ tattve nimittam, abhinnākārāṇāmapi keṣāñcidanyato viśeṣājjātibhedadarśanāt / anyathā hi vilakṣaṇāyā api sāmagrayā avilakṣaṇakāryotpattau na kāraṇabhedābhedābhyāṃ kāryabhedābhedāvityahetukau viśvasya bhedābhedau syātām / tathā hi na bhedādbheda iti abhedādapi nābhedaḥ / tadvyatiriktaśca na kaścidbhāvasvabhāva ityahetukatvādbhāvānāṃ nityaṃ sattvamasattvaṃ vā syāt / apekṣayā hi bhāvāḥ kādācitkā bhavanti / vyavasthāvāṃśca sādhyeṣu sādhananiyogo na syāt / kāraṇaśaktipratiniyame hi kiñcideva kasyacit sādhanāyopādīyeta, nāparaṃ, tasyaiva tatra śakteḥ, anyasya cāśakteḥ tayostajjananetarasvabhāvatvena bhedāt / tajjananasvabhāvavilakṣaṇādapi tasyotpattau na tajjananaśaktipratiniyama iti yat kiñcit yataḥ kutaścitsyāt / tajjananaśaktisāmye tu tadeveti na kāryaṃ duṣṭaṃ kāraṇaṃ vyabhicarati /
body.translated_text: (3.3) [Objection:] But something is observed to arise even from what is of a different kind — for example, lotus roots and the like from cow-dung. — [Reply:] There is no origination from what is of a different kind. For the initial cause of such things is precisely of that kind; hence there is no difference in cause. When occurring in continuous succession, [the plant] arises from the seed. And there is a difference in nature between what is born from cow-dung and what is born otherwise, even when there is no difference in form. For mere similarity of form is not the criterion of the true nature of things, since even among things of similar form, a difference in kind (<s>jāti</s>) is observed due to some other distinguishing characteristic. For otherwise, if even from a cause of different character an effect of similar character were to arise, the difference and non-difference of effects would not be [determined] by the difference and non-difference of causes — and thus the difference and non-difference of the world would be without cause. For if difference does not arise from difference, then non-difference does not arise from non-difference either. And there is no nature of entities other than these two. Therefore, due to being without cause, entities would either always exist or always not exist. For entities are occasional only in dependence [on causes]. And there would be no determinate restriction of means to ends. For if there is a determinate restriction of causal power, only a specific thing would be employed as the means for a specific [end], not another — because that alone has the power for that, and the other lacks it, the two being different through their natures of generating that and not generating it. If something arises even from what is of a nature different from that which generates it, there is no determinate restriction of the power to generate it — and then anything would arise from anything. But if the power to generate that [effect] is equal [in two causes], then they are the same — and so the effect does not deviate from a defective cause.

body.text: (4.1) upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptasyānupalabdhirabhāvasyābhāvavyavahārasya vā hetuḥ / atropalabdherupalabhamānadharmatve tajjñānamupalabdhiḥ / tasmādanyopalabdhiranupalabdhirvivakṣitopalabdheranyatvāt, abhakṣyāsparśanīyavatparyudāsavṛttyā / upalabhyamānadharmatve svaviṣayavijñānajananayogyatālakṣaṇo viṣayasvabhāvaḥ upalabdhiḥ / yogyatāyā bhāvasvarūpatvāt / tasmādanya upalambhajananayogya evānupalabdhiḥ pūrvavat / yatra yasmitrupalabhyamāne niyamena yasyopalabdhiḥ bhavati yogyatāyā aviśeṣāt satatsaṃsṛṣṭaḥ ekajñānasaṃsargāt / tayoḥ satornaikarūpaniyatā pratipattirasambhavāt / tasmādaviśiṣṭayogyatārūpayoḥ ekajñānasaṃsargiṇostayoḥ parasparāpekṣamevānyatvamihābhipretaṃ, pratyāsatterāśrayaṇāt /
body.translated_text: (4.1) Non-perception (<s>anupalabdhi</s>) of what fulfills the conditions of perceptibility (<s>upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta</s>) is the reason (<s>hetu</s>) for [establishing] absence (<s>abhāva</s>) or for the convention of absence (<s>abhāvavyavahāra</s>).
