Here, when 'perception' (<s>upalabdhi</s>) has the property of being what is perceived [i.e., the cognitive side], the cognition of that is 'perception.' Therefore, non-perception is cognition other than that [perception], due to its being different from the intended perception — through the exclusionary mode (<s>paryudāsa</s>), as in [the expressions] 'not to be eaten' and 'not to be touched.' When 'perception' has the property of being what is perceived [i.e., the object-side], 'perception' is the intrinsic nature of the object, characterized by the capacity to generate cognition of its own domain. Because the capacity [to generate cognition] is of the nature of the entity itself. Therefore, non-perception, as before [by the exclusionary mode], is precisely that which is capable of generating apprehension but is [nonetheless] other [than the expected perception]. Where, when some particular [object] that is being perceived is present, the perception of something else necessarily occurs — due to there being no difference in the capacity [to be perceived], that [object] is conjoined with it [the other], through their connection in a single cognition. Because a cognition that does not necessarily have the form of both, when both are present, is impossible. Therefore, for those two [objects] which are of the nature of equal capacity to be perceived and are conjoined in a single cognition, the otherness intended here is only reciprocal — because proximity is what is relied upon.

body.text: sa kevalastadapekṣayā tadanyaśceducyate tadā tajjñānaṃ tatsvabhāvo vā jñātṛjñeya dharmalakṣaṇānupalabdhiḥ / sābhāvaṃ pratiyogino 'bhāvavyavahāraṃ vā sādhayati /
body.translated_text: If that alone, with reference to the other, is called 'different from that,' then the cognition of that [other], or [something] of the nature of that [other], is non-perception characterized by the knower-known-property relation (<s>jñātṛ-jñeya-dharma-lakṣaṇa</s>). It establishes either the [real] absence of the counterpart (<s>pratiyogin</s>) or the convention of absence.

body.text: (4.2) kathamanyabhāvastadabhāvo yena bhāvarūpānupalabdhirabhāvamabhāvavyavahāraṃ vā sādhayediti cet / uktamatra yathā paryudāsavṛttyāpekṣātaḥ tadvivikto 'rthastajjñānaṃ vābhāvo 'nupalabdhiścocyata iti / na pratiṣedhamātraṃ, tasya sādhanāsiddherabhāvavyavahārāsiddhiprasaṅgāt / tasyāsaṃsṛṣṭarūpasya bhāvasiddhirevāparasyābhāvasiddhirityanyabhāvo 'pi tadabhāva iti vyapadiśyate / anyabhāvalakṣaṇo 'bhāvaḥ svayaṃ pramāṇasiddhastadabhāvavyavahāraṃ sādhayet, tatsiddhisiddho veti na kaścidviśeṣo yenānupalabdhyābhāvavyavahārasiddhervirodhaḥ syāt /
body.translated_text: (4.2) [Objection:] How can the existence of something else be the absence of that, such that non-perception in the form of a positive entity would establish absence or the convention of absence? — [Reply:] It has been stated here that through the exclusionary mode (<s>paryudāsa</s>), with reference [to the intended object], a thing distinct from it, or the cognition of it, is called 'absence' and 'non-perception.' [It is] not mere negation, because [if it were mere negation, then] due to the non-establishment of the proof [of mere negation], there would be the unwanted consequence of the non-establishment of the convention of absence. The very establishment of the existence of that [thing] whose form is unconnected [with the counterpart] is the establishment of the absence of the other — therefore, the existence of something else is also designated as 'the absence of that.' Absence characterized by the existence of something else, being itself established by a <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid cognition), would establish the convention of absence of that [counterpart] — or [it could be] established through the establishment of that [positive entity]. There is no difference [between these two] by which there would be any contradiction in establishing the convention of absence through non-perception.

body.text: (4.3) sa evānyabhāvastadviṣayā copalabdhistadabhāvasya kiṃ na sādhanam? kiṃ punarabhāvasya siddhireva tadabhāvasiddhiḥ? iti cet / apṛthaksiddheḥ sambandhābhāvācca /
body.translated_text: (4.3) [Objection:] That very existence of something else and the perception having it as its object — are these not the proof of the absence of that [counterpart]? And is not the establishment of absence itself the establishment of that absence? — [Reply:] Because of non-separate establishment (<s>apṛthaksiddhi</s>), and because of the absence of a [probative] relation.

body.text: anyabhāvastāvatra sādhanam / yatsiddhau yasya na siddhistattasya liṅgaṃ bhavati dhūmāgnivat / anyabhāvasiddhayaiva tadabhāvaḥ prasidhyati, tasya tadanyāsaṃsṛṣṭarūpasya tattvavyavasthāpakena pramāṇenaivānyavyavaccedasiddheḥ /
body.translated_text: The existence of something else is indeed the proof here. That upon whose establishment something [else] is not [yet separately] established — that is the inferential mark (<s>liṅga</s>) of the latter, like smoke and fire. The absence of that [counterpart] is established precisely through the establishment of the existence of something else — because the exclusion of the other is established by the very <s>pramāṇa</s> that determines the reality of that [entity] whose form is unconnected [with the counterpart].

body.text: (4.4) sambandhābhāvācca tacca tasya liṅgaṃ yadi syāt, tasya tena kaścitsambandho bhavet / yathā kṛtakatvasyānityatvena ekārthasamavāyo dhūmasya vā liṅginaikārthasamavāyaḥ / ādhārādheyabhāvo vā janyajanakabhāvo vā / naivaṃ kaścid bhāvābhāvayoḥ sambandhaḥ yenāsyānyabhāvaḥ sādhanaṃ syāt / asti viṣayaviṣayibhāvaḥ śabdārthasambandhavaditi cet / śabdārthayoḥ tatpratipādanābhiprāye sati tatprayogāt kāryakāraṇalakṣaṇo 'vinābhāvalakṣaṇo vā sambandhaḥ syāt / ayaṃ cātra na sambhavati yataḥ viṣayaviṣayibhāvaḥ syāt / siddhe hi tayoḥ sādhyasādhanabhāve tanmukhena viṣayaviṣabhibhāvaḥ syāt / sa eva cāsati sambandhe na sidhyati / anyathetaretarāśrayamidaṃ syāt /
body.translated_text: (4.4) And due to the absence of relation: if that [otherness] were the inferential mark (<s>liṅga</s>) of that [absence], there would have to be some relation between them—as, for example, the co-inherence in a single object (<s>ekārthasamavāya</s>) of being produced (<s>kṛtakatva</s>) with impermanence, or of smoke with the inferential subject (<s>liṅgin</s>); or the relation of support and supported (<s>ādhārādheyabhāva</s>), or the relation of produced and producer (<s>janyajanakabhāva</s>). But no such relation exists between [positive] existence and [negative] non-existence by which otherness (<s>anyabhāva</s>) could be the means of proving [absence]. [Objection:] There is the relation of object and cognizer (<s>viṣayaviṣayibhāva</s>), like the relation between a word and its meaning. [Reply:] Between a word and its meaning, when there is the intention of conveying that [meaning], due to its use for that purpose, there would be a relation characterized by cause and effect or by invariable concomitance (<s>avinābhāva</s>). But this is not possible here, from which the object-cognizer relation would [follow]. For only when the relation of probandum and means of proof between them is [already] established would the object-cognizer relation hold through that. But that very [relation] is not established in the absence of a [prior] relation. Otherwise, this would be a case of mutual dependence (<s>itaretarāśraya</s>).

body.text: (4.5) anyabhāvāccābhāvasiddhāvasamudāyaśca sādhyaḥ syāt / tathā ca ghaṭābhāvastadanyabhāvāt iti ghaṭasya sarvatra sarvadā cābhāvaḥ prasajyeta / na, pradeśādirdharmī ghaṭābhāvena viśeṣyata iti tadviśeṣaṇabhūto 'bhāvaḥ sādhyate na tu kevalaḥ / tato nāsamudāyasya sādhyatā / na ca liṅgaliṅganorasambandhaḥ, anyabhāvasya pradeśādinā sambandhād iti cet / na, pradeśāderevānyabhāvatvāt / yatraiva hi pradeśādau yatrāstīti ucyate sa eva tenāsaṃsṛṣṭo 'nyabhāvaḥ / taddarśanādevāsya ghaṭo nāsti iti vikalpo bhavati iti kathaṃ tasyaiva liṅgaliṅgibhāvaḥ?
body.translated_text: (4.5) And if absence is proved from otherness, even a non-aggregate would be what is to be proved. Thus, "the absence of a pot is due to the presence of what is other than it"—the absence of the pot would follow everywhere and at all times. [Reply:] No, because the property-bearer—a particular location etc.—is qualified by the absence of the pot; so it is the absence as a qualifier of that [location] that is proved, not [absence] by itself. Therefore the non-aggregate is not what is to be proved. [Objection:] There is no absence of relation between the mark and the marked, since otherness has a relation with the location etc. [Reply:] No, because the location etc. itself is the otherness. For the very location etc. where it is said "it exists here"—that itself, unconnected with [the pot], is the otherness. Since it is from the perception of that very [location] that the conceptual cognition (<s>vikalpa</s>) "the pot does not exist here" arises, how can that itself have the relationship of mark and marked (<s>liṅgaliṅgibhāva</s>)?

body.text: (4.6) na cātra sāmānyaviśeṣabhāvakalpanā sambhavati yena sāmānyaṃ heturbhaved viśeṣo dharmāti, tadviśeṣapratipattereva tadabhāvasya pratīteḥ, tasyānyatrānvayasyābhāvāt pratijñārthaikadeśatvācca na hetutā / na ca yatra pradeśamātraṃ tatra ghaṭābhāvaḥ / tādṛśe kevale pradeśe sarvatrābhāva iti cet / nanu tasyaiva kaivalyaṃ ghaṭavirahaḥ / sa ca tatpratipattāveva siddha iti kasya idānīṃ talliṅgam? anvayasyānugamanamapi nirarthakam / tasmādanyabhāvo na sādhanamabhāvasya /
body.translated_text: (4.6) Nor is the postulation of a universal-particular relation (<s>sāmānyaviśeṣabhāva</s>) possible here, such that the universal would be the reason and the particular the property—because the cognition of absence arises from the cognition of that very particular [otherness]; because of the absence of its positive concomitance (<s>anvaya</s>) elsewhere; and because, being a part of the thesis-meaning (<s>pratijñārthaikadeśa</s>), it cannot serve as the reason. Nor is there absence of a pot wherever there is mere location. [Objection:] In such a bare location, there is absence everywhere. [Reply:] But the very bareness [of that location] is the absence of the pot. And that is established just by the cognition of that [bare location]. So whose inferential mark is this now? Even the tracing of positive concomitance is pointless. Therefore, otherness (<s>anyabhāva</s>) is not the means of proving absence.

body.text: (4.7) asti virodhaḥ sambandhaḥ tato 'nyabhāvādabhāvasya siddhiḥ iti cet / kena kasya virodho 'nyabhāvena pratiyoginaḥ kiṃ nu vai pratiyogī pramātumiṣṭo yena liṅgaliṅganorvirodhaḥ sambandhaḥ syāt? abhāvastupratiyogino ghaṭasya anyabhāvena aviruddhaḥ sahāvasthānāt / tasmin prameye liṅgaliṅginoḥ kathaṃ virodhaḥ? tasmātsambandhābhāvaḥ / atrāpi asamudāyasādhyatvaṃ tadavastham /
body.translated_text: (4.7) [Objection:] There is a relation of opposition (<s>virodha</s>); therefore the establishment of absence is from otherness. [Reply:] Opposition of what with what? With otherness, of the counter-correlate (<s>pratiyogin</s>)—is the counter-correlate intended to be the object of proof, such that the opposition between the mark and the marked would serve as the relation? But the absence of the counter-correlate, the pot, is not incompatible with otherness, since they co-exist. In the case of that provable [proposition], how is there opposition between the mark and the marked? Therefore, there is no relation. Here too, the charge of proving a non-aggregate remains the same.

body.text: (4.8) nanu anyabhāvatadabhāvayorasati sambandhe 'nyabhāvagatyāpi tadabhāvagatirna syāditi cet / na vai kutaścit sambandhādanyabhāvastadabhāvagamaka iṣṭaḥ kintu anyabhāva eva tadabhāvo yathoktaṃ prāk / tasyānyāsaṃsṛṣṭarūpasya kevalasyaikātmavyasthitasya tadātmanā pariccedasyaivānyavyavaccedatvāt tasya kaivalyamevāparasya vaikalyamiti tadanyabhāva eva tadabhāvaḥ / tataśca tatpratipattireva tadapratipattiḥ / anyathā tasya pariccedena tato 'nyasya avyavaccede tatparicceda eva na syāt / tadatadrūpayoravivekāt / ya eva vyavahāraḥ kasyacitkvaceddeśe darśanāt prāptiparihārārthaḥ sa na syāt / na hyayamanalaṃ paśyatrapi kevalam analameva paśyatīti kathaṃ salilārthī tatra na praverteta? anupalambhena salilābhāvaḥ pratīyata iti cet / ko 'yamanupalambho nāma? yadi salilopalambhābhāvaḥ tadā kathamabhāvaḥ kasyacitpratipattiḥ pratipattiheturvā? tasyāpi kathaṃ pratipattiḥ? tasya tato vānyasya kasyacidapyapratipattāvapi yadyabhāvaḥ pratīyate tadā svāpamadamūrccāvyavadhānapṛṣṭhībhāvādyavasthāsvapi kiṃ na pratīyate? ityetacca vicāritaṃ pramāṇaviniścaye / tasmādayamanalaṃ paśyatrapi analo 'yaṃ salilam iti nādhyavasyatīti na tiṣṭhetrāpi pratiṣṭheta / tataśca dustaraṃ vyasanaṃ pratipattuḥ syāt /
body.translated_text: (4.8) [Objection:] If there is no relation between the existence of one thing and the non-existence of another, then even through the cognition of the existence of one thing, the cognition of the non-existence of the other would not follow. — [Reply:] It is not from some [external] relation that the existence of one thing is held to indicate the non-existence of the other; rather, the existence of one thing is itself the non-existence of the other, as stated before. For since the determination of that [entity] — which is unmixed with others in nature, existing alone, established in a single self — as being of its own nature is itself the exclusion of others, its aloneness is itself the absence of the other. Thus the existence of one thing is itself the non-existence of the other. And therefore, the cognition of it is itself the non-cognition of the other. Otherwise, if through the determination of one thing, the other is not excluded from it, then the determination of the one would itself not be possible — because of the non-differentiation between what is of that nature and what is not. The very practical activity (<s>vyavahāra</s>) of approaching and avoiding, based on seeing something at a certain location, would not be possible. For this person sees only fire — he perceives nothing but fire — so why would a person seeking water not approach [that location]? [Objection:] Through non-perception (<s>anupalambha</s>), the absence of water is cognized. — [Reply:] What is this 'non-perception'? If it is the absence of the perception of water, then how is absence — which is the cognition of something or the cause of cognition — itself cognized? And how is that too cognized? If absence is cognized even without the cognition of it or of anything else whatsoever, then why is it not cognized in states of sleep, intoxication, fainting, obstruction, turning away, and the like? — This has been examined in the <s>Pramāṇaviniścaya</s>. Therefore, this person who sees only fire does not determine that 'this fire is water' — so he would not remain even where he stands. And thus, an insuperable calamity would befall the cognizer.

body.text: (4.9) tata evaikasya darśanād anyābhāvagatiścet kathamekaṃ dṛṣṭamanyatrāstīti pratyāyayati? tasyaiva kevalasya darśanād iti cet / idamevāsmābhiḥ prāgabhihitaṃ kasmāttavātra paruṣamivābhāti? tasmāttīrādarśineva śakuninā dūraparyaṭayāpi pratyāgantavyamityalam avidyamānapratiṣṭhānayā diśaḥ pratipattyā /
body.translated_text: (4.9) [Objection:] If the cognition of the absence of others [follows] from seeing one thing alone, then how does something seen [in one place] make [others] understand that it exists elsewhere? [Reply:] From seeing that very thing alone. — [Objection:] This is exactly what we have stated before — why does it seem harsh to you here? Therefore, like a bird that does not see the shore, even after wandering far, one must return [to the starting point]. Enough of this running in a direction that has no footing.

body.text: (4.10) yadyekapariccedādevānyavyavaccedaḥ sidhyati tadā sarvasyānyasya aviśeṣeṇa tatrābhāvasiddhirbhavet / na tu tulyayogyāvasthasyaiva / upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptasyānupalabdhirabhāvasādhanīti ca viśeṣaṇaṃ na vaktavyam, anupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptānāmapi tatra vyavaccedāt /
body.translated_text: (4.10) [Objection:] If the exclusion of the other is accomplished merely from the determination of one thing, then the absence of everything else without distinction would be established there. But [we hold] only [the absence] of what is in an equal state of fitness. And the qualification 'non-perception of what fulfills the conditions of perceptibility (<s>upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta</s>) is the means of establishing absence' need not be stated — since even those that fulfill the conditions of non-perceptibility are excluded from there.

body.text: (4.11) ekātmapariccedāt tasya tadanyātmavyavaccedo bhavati tadātmaniyatapratibhāsajñānāt na hi tadātmā tadanyasyātmā bhavati / anyātmāvyavaccede pravṛttinivṛttyoḥ abhāva iti pūrvaḥ prasaṅgaḥ / taṃ ca deśakālasvabhāvāvasthāniyataṃ tadātmanopalabhamānā buddhiḥ tathātvapracyutimasya vyavaccinati / evaṃ hi taddeśādiniyataḥ pariccitro bhavati, yadi anyathābhāvo vyavaccinno bhavatiḥ tathātvaṃ ca tasyaiva bhavati nānyasyeti anyathābhūtāttathābhūtaṃ vyavaccindatyeva tat pariccinati / evamekapramāṇavṛttiḥ sarvabhāvān dvairāśye vyavasthāpayati / tasyānvayavyatirekabuddhijanakatvenaiva sāphalyāt / tadvayatiriktāśeṣavyavaccedena vyāptisādhanādeva prakārāntarasyābhāvaḥ sidhyati / tasya tadanyatayā vyāptyabhāve tena tadarthāvyavaccedātpunarapi bhāvasyāpariccedaprasaṅgāt /
body.translated_text: (4.11) From the determination of one thing as being of its own nature, there is the exclusion of its being of the nature of another — because of the cognition whose appearance is restricted to its own nature. For the nature of one thing is not the nature of another. In the absence of the exclusion of the other's nature, there would be an absence of [both] activity and withdrawal — which is the earlier absurd consequence [already discussed]. And the cognition that apprehends it as restricted to [a particular] location, time, nature, and state excludes its deviation from such-ness. For it is determined as restricted to that location and so forth only if its being-otherwise is excluded. And such-ness belongs to that very [entity] and not to another — therefore [the cognition] that excludes the otherwise-being from the such-being does indeed determine it. Thus, a single operation of a <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid cognition) establishes all entities in a twofold classification — because its efficacy consists precisely in generating cognitions of positive and negative concomitance (<s>anvaya-vyatireka</s>). The absence of any third alternative is established precisely through the establishment of pervasion by the exhaustive exclusion of everything other than those two. For in the absence of the pervasion of that [entity] by its being other [than the third alternative], through the non-exclusion of that [third alternative] from it, there would again be the absurd consequence of the entity's non-determination.

body.text: (4.12) tasmātkvacitpramāṇaṃ pravṛttaṃ tat pariccinatti, tadanyad vyavaccināti, tṛtīyaprakārābhāvaṃ ca sūcayati iti ekapramāṇavyāpāra eṣaḥ / tathāhi kvacitpramāṇaṃ pravṛtaṃ tadeva tadanyasmād vyavaccinattī, tasyaiva pariccedāt / tadanyadeva ca tasmād vyavaccinatti anyasya tatra apariccedāt / atastadeva pramāṇaṃ prakārāntabhāvaṃ sādhayati, tasmin dṛṣṭatadanyatvena sarvasyaiva vyasthāpanāt, atadanyasyaiva ca tattvena vyavasthāpanāt /
body.translated_text: (4.12) Therefore, a <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid cognition) that operates on something determines it, excludes what is other than it, and also indicates the absence of a third alternative — and this is a single operation of the <s>pramāṇa</s>. For a <s>pramāṇa</s> that operates on something excludes that very thing from what is other than it — because of its determination [as being that thing]. And it excludes what is other from that — because of the non-determination of the other in it. Therefore, that very <s>pramāṇa</s> establishes the absence of a third alternative, because everything is established as being either identical with or different from that which is seen, and because only what is not different from it is established as being of that nature.

body.text: etena kramākramādayo 'pyanyonyavyavaccedarūpā vyākhytāḥ /
body.translated_text: By this, sequence (<s>krama</s>), simultaneity (<s>akrama</s>), and other [relations] too, which are of the nature of mutual exclusion, are explained.

body.text: tadevamekasyopalambhāttasya tadanyātmano vyavaccedaḥ / na taddeśakālayoḥ sarvasyānyasya bhāvasya vyavaccedaḥ / tasmādatadatmā ca syāttaddeśakālaśca, rasarūpādivat / tasmādyathoktādevānupalambhātkvacit kadācitkasyacidabhāvasiddhiḥ /
body.translated_text: Thus, from the apprehension (<s>upalambha</s>) of one thing, the exclusion of what is of a nature different from it [follows]. But this does not mean the exclusion of every other entity at that place and time. Therefore, something could be of a different nature [from the apprehended thing] and yet exist at that same place and time — like taste, color, and the like. Therefore, the establishment of the absence of something, somewhere, at some time, is only from non-apprehension (<s>anupalambha</s>) as described.

body.text: (4.13) anyabhāvaviṣayasyopalabdhirapi tadabhāvasya sādhikeṣṭaiva na tu liṅgatvena / tatrāpyabhāvasya pṛthak sādhyatve sambandhābhāvasya tulyatvāt / liṅgāvirbhāvakāla eva tadabhāvasiddheśca / na hi anyasya bhāvaṃ pratipadya tatpratipatteḥ anvayavyatirekau prasādhya tadabhāvaṃ pratipadyate / kiṃ tarhi? tadanyaṃ pratipadyamāna eva tadabhāvaṃ pratipadyate / darśanānantaram idamasti idaṃ tu nāsti iti vyavasthāpanāt / tacca tasya liṅgaṃ bhavati yasyānvayi vyatireko ca / dṛṣṭāntāsiddheḥ / na hi evaṃ śakyaṃ darśayituṃ yatra anyabhāvopalabdhistatra tadabhāvaḥ iti / tadekopalabdheḥ kvacidapyabhāvāt / sāmānyena pradarśane dṛṣṭānte 'pi pramāṇāntaraṃ nāsti, kiṃtu saiva tadanyabhāvopalabdhiḥ sādhyadharmasya sādhiketi anavasthā dṛṣṭāntānāmityapratipattiḥ / tasmāt naiva kutaścilliṅgāt tadabhāvasiddhiḥ / so 'nyabhāvaḥ pratyakṣalakṣaṇenānupalambhena siddhaḥ san mūḍhapratipattāvabhāvavyavahāraṃ sādhayed iti alaṃ prasaṅgena /
body.translated_text: (4.13) The apprehension of a different entity is also desired as establishing the absence of that [other entity], but not as a logical mark (<s>liṅga</s>). For therein too, when absence is to be separately established, the absence of the relation is equally [problematic]. Moreover, the establishment of that absence occurs at the very time of the appearance of the logical mark. For one does not first cognize the existence of another entity, then establish the positive and negative concomitance of that cognition, and then cognize the absence of that [entity]. Rather, in the very act of cognizing the other [entity], one cognizes the absence of that [entity] — because of the determination immediately after seeing: "this exists, but that does not exist." And that is the logical mark of something for which there is both positive and negative concomitance — but the example (<s>dṛṣṭānta</s>) is unestablished. For it cannot be shown thus: "wherever there is apprehension of a different entity, there is absence of that [entity]" — because that single entity being apprehended is nowhere absent. If shown by a generality, even in the example there is no other means of valid knowledge; rather, that very apprehension of the different entity is the establisher of the property to be proved — and so there would be an infinite regress (<s>anavasthā</s>) of examples, hence non-understanding. Therefore, the absence of that [entity] is never established from any logical mark whatsoever. That different entity, being established through non-apprehension characterized by direct perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>), may establish the convention of absence for a confused cognizer — but enough with this digression.

body.text: (4.14) seyamanupalabdhistridhā / siddhe kāryakāraṇabhāve siddhābhāvasya kāraṇasyānupalabdhiḥ, vyāpyavyāpakabhāvasiddhau siddhābhāvasya vyāpakasyānupalabdhiḥ svabhāvānupalabdhiśca / tatra kāraṇavyāpakayorapi abhāvavyavahāraḥ tadanyabhāvasiddhayaiva sidhyati / sa tathā siddhaḥ san kāryavyāpyayorabhāvam abhāvavyavahāraṃ vā sādhayati / svabhāvānupalabdhau tu anupalabdhyā liṅgabhūtayā abhāvavyavahāra eva sādhyate /
body.translated_text: (4.14) This non-apprehension (<s>anupalabdhi</s>) is threefold: (1) when the cause-effect relation is established, the non-apprehension of the cause whose absence is established; (2) when the pervaded-pervader relation (<s>vyāpya-vyāpaka-bhāva</s>) is established, the non-apprehension of the pervader whose absence is established; and (3) the non-apprehension of essential nature (<s>svabhāvānupalabdhi</s>). Among these, the convention of absence regarding the cause and the pervader is established only through the establishment of a different entity. That [different entity], being thus established, establishes the absence or the convention of absence of the effect and the pervaded. But in the non-apprehension of essential nature, the convention of absence alone is what is established by the non-apprehension that functions as the logical mark.

body.text: (4.15) yadi kāraṇavyāpakau tadanyabhāvasiddhayānupalabdhyā siddhāsad vyavahārāvanyasyābhāvamabhāvavyavahāṃra ca sādhayataḥ / sā ca tayorupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptāvevāsadvyavahārasya sādhiketi kathaṃ tayoḥ parokṣe 'rtheprayogaḥ? naiva prayogaḥ pramāṇatayā, liṇgasyāniścayāt / kevalaṃ kāraṇavyāpakayorhi siddhasambandhayoryadyabhāvaḥ parasyāpi avaśyamabhāvaḥ iti etasya darśanārthamete prayujyete iti / eṣa eva pakṣadharmo 'nvayavyatirekavān iti tadaṃśena vyāptaḥ trilakṣaṇa eva trividha eva heturgamakaḥ svaśādhyadharmāvyabhicārāt /
body.translated_text: (4.15) If the [non-apprehension of] the cause and the pervader — having established the convention of non-existence through non-apprehension that is itself established by the establishment of a different entity — establish the absence and convention of absence of something else; and if that [non-apprehension] establishes the convention of non-existence only when the conditions for apprehension of those [cause/pervader] are met — then how can they be applied to a remote object? [Reply:] They are not applied as means of valid knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>), since the logical mark is uncertain. Rather, these are applied only to show that if the cause and the pervader, whose relation is established, are absent, then necessarily the other [effect/pervaded] is also absent. This very property of the thesis-subject (<s>pakṣadharma</s>), possessing positive and negative concomitance and pervaded by that aspect — [constitutes] the three-marked (<s>trilakṣaṇa</s>), threefold logical reason (<s>hetu</s>) that is inferential, due to the non-deviation from its own provable property.

body.text: (5.1) ṣaḍliṅgo heturityapare / trīṇi caitāni abādhitaviṣayatvaṃ vivakṣitaikasaṃkhyatvaṃ jñātatvaṃ ceti / tatrābādhitaviṣayatvaṃ tāvat pṛthag lakṣaṇaṃ na bhavati, bādhāvinābhāvayorvirodhāt / avinābhāvo hi satyeva sādhyadharme bhāvo hetoḥ / sa hetustallakṣaṇaḥ dharmiṇi syād atra ca sādhyadharmaḥ kathaṃ na bhavet? pratyakṣānumāne hi sādhyadharmaṃ bādhamāne taṃ dharmiṇo niṣkāsayataḥ tasmiṃśca satyeva heturbhavan taṃ tatraivāvasthāpayatīti paraṃ bata bhāvānāmasvāsthyam /
body.translated_text: (5.1) Others [say] the logical reason (<s>hetu</s>) has six marks (<s>liṅga</s>). And these three [additional ones] are: having an uncontradicted subject-matter (<s>abādhita-viṣayatva</s>), having the desired singular number (<s>vivakṣita-eka-saṃkhyatva</s>), and being known (<s>jñātatva</s>). Among these, first, having an uncontradicted subject-matter is not a separate mark, because of the contradiction between contradiction (<s>bādhā</s>) and inseparability (<s>avinābhāva</s>). For inseparability means the presence of the logical reason only when the provable property exists. That logical reason, characterized by that [inseparability], would be present in the thesis-subject (<s>dharmin</s>) — and how then could the provable property not be present there? For when perception and inference contradict the provable property, they remove it from the thesis-subject; but the logical reason, existing precisely when that [provable property] exists, establishes it right there — what great instability of entities indeed!

body.text: anyatra sādhyadharmeṇāvinābhāvī heturna punaḥ sādhyadharmiṇeveti cet / tat kimayaṃ tapasvī śaṇḍhamudvāhya putraṃ mṛgayate? yasya dharmiṇyasatyapi sādhyadharme bhāvaḥ, tamupadarśya kathaṃ sa dharmī sādhyadharmavānityucyate?
body.translated_text: [Objection:] The logical reason is inseparable from the provable property elsewhere, but not necessarily in the thesis-subject itself. — [Reply:] Does this ascetic, having married a eunuch, seek a son? By pointing out a logical reason that is present even when the provable property is absent in the thesis-subject, how can one say that the thesis-subject possesses the provable property?

body.text: (5.2) ata eva bādhābhāva uktaḥ / syādetad, yata eva heturanyathāpi bhavedata eva pramāṇābhyāmabādhitadharmā dharmītyucyata iti /
body.translated_text: (5.2) For this very reason, the absence of contradiction (<s>bādhā</s>) was mentioned. [Objection:] It might be that the thesis-subject is said to have the uncontradicted property precisely because the logical reason could also be otherwise.

body.text: tatkimidānīṃ hetoḥ sāmarthyam? abādhayaiva sādhyasiddhervyartho hetuḥ / bādhāyāmapi sādhyābhāvasya tena sādhanāt kutaḥ sādhanasya sāmarthyam / aniyame bādhakapramāṇavṛttau sādhyābhāvasya, bādhakapramāṇasyābhāvaḥ sādhyābhāvasya ca saṃbhavaḥ syāditi na sāmarthyamabādhāyāḥ /
body.translated_text: Then what is the efficacy (<s>sāmarthya</s>) of the reason now? Since the <s>sādhya</s> (probandum) is established by non-sublation (<s>abādhā</s>) alone, the reason is pointless. Even in the case of sublation (<s>bādhā</s>), since the absence of the probandum is proved by that [sublation], whence the efficacy of the means of proof? When the occurrence of sublating evidence (<s>bādhakapramāṇa</s>) is undetermined regarding the absence of the probandum, there could be both the absence of sublating evidence and the possibility of the absence of the probandum—therefore non-sublation does not possess efficacy.

body.text: (5.3) na bādhāyā abhāvo 'bādhā / kiṃ tarhi? bādhāyā anupalabdhiḥ sā ca puruṣasya kvacid bādhāyāḥ saṃbhave 'pi syāditi sa hetuprayogasya viṣayaḥ / kiṃ nu vai heturbādhopalabdherbibheti na punarbādhāyā yena bādhāmanādṛtya tadanupalabdhau prayoktavya iṣṭaḥ? sa tarhi paramārthena- 'bādhā kimasti nāsti' ityanapekṣya bādhāyā anupalabdhau prayoktavyaḥ? kimarthaṃ prayujyate? sādhyasiddhayartham / sa kiṃ kvacit satyāmapi bādhāyāṃ sādhyaṃ sādhayed yenāsyā abhāvaniścayaṃ prati yatno na kriyate hetuśca pratyujyate / evaṃ ca sati abādhitaviṣayatvaṃ hetulakṣaṇaṃ na bhavati / bādhāyāmapi satyāmasya sāmarthyāt / tathā ca saṃśayitasya pravṛttirna yujyate / yathā ca bādhānupalabdhau tāmabhyupagamya prayujyate tathā tadupalabdhāvapi prayujyatām, abhyupagame viśeṣābhāvāt /
body.translated_text: (5.3) Non-sublation is not the absence of sublation. Then what? It is the non-perception (<s>anupalabdhi</s>) of sublation. And that [non-perception] could exist for a person even when sublation is possible in some case—so that is the domain of the application of the reason. Does the reason then fear the perception of sublation, such that it is desired to be applied only upon non-perception of sublation, disregarding sublation itself? Then is it to be applied ultimately—without regard to whether sublation exists or not—upon the non-perception of sublation? For what purpose is it applied? For the establishment of the probandum. Does it establish the probandum even when sublation is present in some case, such that no effort is made toward ascertaining its absence and the reason is still applied? If so, having an uncontradicted subject-matter (<s>abādhitaviṣayatva</s>) would not be a characteristic of the reason, since it has efficacy even when sublation is present. And thus, proceeding when in doubt is not proper. Just as when sublation is not perceived, [the reason] is applied accepting that [non-sublation], so too let it be applied even when [sublation] is perceived, since there is no difference in the acceptance.

body.text: (5.4) na bādhāyāṃ satyāṃ hetoḥ sāmarthyamiti cet / yadyevam, anirṇītabādhāsambhavo hetuḥ prayogaṃ hārhati, mā bhūt bādhāyāḥ saṃbhavapakṣe prayuktasyāpyasāmarthyamiti /
body.translated_text: (5.4) [Objection:] The reason does not have efficacy when sublation is present. [Reply:] If so, a reason whose possibility of sublation is not determined deserves not to be applied, lest even when applied in the case where sublation is possible, it be without efficacy.

body.text: bādhānupalambhe sati sāmarthyamiti cet / kimupalambho bādhāṃ vyāpnoti, yato hetorbādhāsambhavakṛtam asāmarthyaṃ na sambhavet? atha tannivṛttau bādhā nivartate / tathāpi bādhānupalambhādeva sādhyāsiddhervyartho hetuḥ / anupalambhe bādhāyā asambhavāt / upalambhasya nivṛttāvapi bādhāyā anivṛttau tadavasthaṃ hetorasāmarthyamityaprayogaḥ / tasmāt svasādhyabhāvābhāvādhyāmanyathāpi bhavanhetuḥ dharmiṇi na kiñcidbhāvayati na vibhāvayati iti tadupakṣepo na samarthaḥ / iti bādhāvinābhāvayorvirodhaḥ / tatrābādhā rūpāntaram /
body.translated_text: [Objection:] The efficacy exists when sublation is not perceived. [Reply:] Does perception pervade sublation, such that the incapacity of the reason caused by the possibility of sublation would not arise? If sublation ceases when perception ceases—even so, the reason is pointless, since the probandum is not established through mere non-perception of sublation, because sublation does not occur when there is non-perception. Even when perception ceases, if sublation does not cease, the incapacity of the reason remains the same, and so it should not be applied. Therefore, a reason that can be otherwise regarding the existence or non-existence of its own probandum neither establishes nor disestablishes anything in the property-bearer (<s>dharmin</s>)—hence its mention is not capable [of proving anything]. Thus there is a contradiction between sublation (<s>bādhā</s>) and invariable concomitance (<s>avinābhāva</s>). Therein, non-sublation is a different form [of the same].

body.text: (5.5) tatrāma tasmād viśeṣaṇāntaraṃ bhavet lakṣaṇāntaratvena copādānamarhati yasya bhāve 'pi yasya aparasyābhāvaḥ syāt / tadyathā pakṣadharmatvaṃ sapakṣe ca bhāva iti / n acaitad abādhāyā avinābhāve sati sambhavati iti na sādhyaviparyayāvinābhāvinorhetuviruddhayorviṣaye bādhā saṃbhavati iti na tadabhāvaḥ pṛthaganayorlakṣaṇāntaratvena vācyaḥ / tasmād hetoḥ prayoge pratijñādoṣāṇāṃ saṃbhavo nāsti / nāpi kevalā pratijñaiva prayujyate / tataśca na pratijñādoṣā vācyāḥ /
body.translated_text: (5.5) Therefore, it should be a different qualification and deserves to be taken up as a distinct characteristic—[namely that qualification] in whose presence the absence of the other occurs. That is: the property of the thesis-subject (<s>pakṣadharmatva</s>) and the occurrence in the homologous instance (<s>sapakṣa</s>). And this is not possible when there is invariable concomitance of non-sublation—therefore sublation does not arise in the domain of the reason and what contradicts the probandum (<s>sādhyaviparyaya</s>). Therefore, the absence of that [sublation] need not be stated separately as a distinct characteristic. Hence, in the application of the reason, there is no possibility of thesis-defects (<s>pratijñādoṣa</s>). Nor is a bare thesis alone applied. Therefore, thesis-defects are not to be stated.

body.text: (5.6) etena ekasaṃkhyāvivakṣāpi pratyuktā /
body.translated_text: (5.6) By this, the desire for specifying a single number is also answered.

body.text: katham? eko hi hetuḥ svasādhyabhāva eva bhavediti tatrāvyabhicārī tatraiva tasmādanyo 'pi kathaṃ heturbhavati? ekasya yat sādhyaṃ tadabādhakasya dharmasya bhāva eva bhāvāditi bādhayā samānam /
body.translated_text: How? For one reason would exist only in the presence of its own probandum, and being non-deviating (<s>avyabhicārin</s>) there—how then could another also be a reason for that very [probandum]? The existence of a property that does not sublate the probandum of one [reason]—existing only where its own probandum exists—is the same as sublation.

body.text: (5.7) api ca / kiṃ yo vastuto 'sambhavatpratihetuḥ sa samyagjñānasya viparyayasya vā heturiṣṭa āhosvidapradarśitapratihetuḥ? kiṃ cātaḥ?
body.translated_text: (5.7) Moreover: is the counter-reason (<s>pratihetu</s>) that is actually impossible the cause of correct knowledge or of erroneous knowledge? Or [is the question about] the counter-reason that has not been demonstrated? And what follows from that?

body.text: yadyasambhavatpratihetuḥ aśakyaniścayatvādalakṣaṇametad hetvabhāvo vā / na hi aniścitātmanaḥ pratipādakadharmasya tallakṣaṇatvaṃ yathā sandigdhasya pakṣadharmatvasya / nāpi sandigdhalakṣaṇo heturbhavediti na kaścid heturbhavet / tulye lakṣaṇe di dṛṣṭaḥ pratiyoginaḥ saṃbhavo 'dṛṣṭapratiyogiṣu api śaṃkāmutpādayati viśeṣābhāvāt / sati vā viśeṣe sa viśeṣo hetorlakṣaṇam / yatastadviśeṣād heturekāntena nirastapratipakṣaḥ svasādhyaṃ niścāyayatīti atallakṣaṇo na hetuḥ syāt tathā ca vyarthā ekasaṃkhyāvivakṣā / ato viruddhāvyabhicāriṇo lakṣaṇaṃ hīyeta svalakṣaṇayuktayorhetvorekatra dharmiṇi virodhenopanipāte sati viruddhāvyabhicārī iti /
body.translated_text: If [the pseudo-reason is defined as one] whose counter-reason is impossible — then, because it is impossible to ascertain [impossibility], this is either not a [valid] defining characteristic, or [amounts to] the absence of a reason altogether. For a demonstrating property (<s>pratipādakadharma</s>) whose nature is uncertain cannot serve as a defining characteristic — just as a doubtful property of the thesis-subject (<s>pakṣadharmatva</s>) [cannot]. Nor could a reason with a doubtful defining characteristic be a reason at all — [and so] no reason whatsoever would exist. For when the defining characteristic is the same, the observed possibility of a counter-reason [in one case] raises suspicion even in [cases with] unobserved counter-reasons, due to the absence of any distinguishing feature. Or, if there is a distinguishing feature, that distinguishing feature is the defining characteristic of the reason. Since by virtue of that distinguishing feature, the reason conclusively, with its counter-reason eliminated, establishes its own <s>sādhya</s> (what is to be proved) — [then] what lacks that defining characteristic would not be a reason; and so the intention to designate [anything as] a single [type of pseudo-reason] would be pointless. Therefore, the definition of the <s>viruddhāvyabhicārin</s> (contradictory non-deviating [pseudo-reason]) would fail — [for it is defined as follows:] when two reasons, each possessing their own defining characteristics, occur in a single property-bearer (<s>dharmin</s>) in mutual contradiction, that is the <s>viruddhāvyabhicārin</s>.

body.text: (5.8) na ca tasya viśeṣasya svarūpaṃ nirdiṣṭaṃ, yadrūpaṃ pratītya pratiyoginaḥ sambhavāsambhavāvutpaśyāmaḥ / tasmātrāstyevaṃ viśeṣa iti sarvatra śaṅkayā bhavitavyam /
body.translated_text: (5.8) And the intrinsic nature of that distinguishing feature has not been specified — the nature upon which we would judge the possibility or impossibility of the counter-reason. Therefore, there must be doubt everywhere that 'such a distinguishing feature exists.'

body.text: dṛṣṭapratihetorapi hetoḥ prāgitareṇa na kaścidviśeṣo lakṣyate / na ca saṃbhavatpratihetūnāmapi sarvadā tasyopalabdhiḥ / atiśayavatī tu prajñā pratihetūtprekṣiṇī dṛṣṭā / tenāniścayaḥ pratiyoginaḥ saṃbhavāsaṃbhavayoriti vastuto / sambhavatpratihetutvalakṣaṇasya aniścitatvātra kaścid hetuḥ syāt /
body.translated_text: Even in the case of a reason for which a counter-reason has been observed, no distinguishing feature from the other [reasons] is perceived prior [to the observation]. Nor is that [distinguishing feature] always perceived even in [cases where] counter-reasons are possible. Indeed, it is only an exceptionally keen intellect that has been observed to envision counter-reasons. Therefore, in reality, there is uncertainty regarding the possibility and impossibility of the counter-reason. Since the defining characteristic of 'having a possible counter-reason' is itself uncertain — [on this view] no reason whatsoever could exist.

body.text: (5.9) athāpradarśitapratihetuḥ yathāha, "yadā tarhi śabdatvaṃ nityamabhyupagaccati tadāyaṃ hetureva syād yadyatra anityatvahetuṃ kṛtakatvādi kaścitra darśayed " iti / idamidānīṃ sumahad vyasanamāyātaṃ gurubhirabhihitatvādaprakāśyaṃ, nyāyamanupālayadbhirasaṃvaraṇīyamiti kaṣṭataraṃ vyasanaṃ kathaṃ nirvoḍhuṃ śakyeta? sa tāvadayaṃ hetuḥ vastūni svasādhyaprakṛtīni kṛtvā tatpramāṇakān puruṣān abhyudayaniḥ śreyasābhyāṃ yojayitvā punaśca pratibhāvatā puruṣeṇa hetvantaranidarśanena utkīlitasādhanasāmarthyaḥ tāni vastūni tadbhāvasampadastāṃśca puruṣān abhyudayaniḥ śreyasasampadaḥ pracyāvya bhraṣṭarājya iva rājā tapovanaṃ gaccatīti kimatra brūmaḥ /
body.translated_text: (5.9) Now, [consider the pseudo-reason defined as one] whose counter-reason has not been demonstrated — as [the opponent] states: 'When one accepts sound-hood (<s>śabdatva</s>) as permanent, this would indeed be a reason — provided someone could demonstrate a reason for impermanence, such as being-produced (<s>kṛtakatva</s>), somewhere here.' Now a very great calamity has arrived — it cannot be revealed because it was stated by the venerable teachers, yet since those who uphold logic cannot conceal it — how can this most painful calamity be endured? This reason, having made things into entities of the nature of its own <s>sādhya</s> (what is to be proved) and having connected the persons who take it as their <s>pramāṇa</s> with worldly prosperity and ultimate good — then, when its proving capacity is uprooted by a brilliant person's demonstration of another reason, those things [lose] their attainment of that nature, and those persons [lose] their attainment of worldly prosperity and ultimate good — like a king who has lost his kingdom, [the reason] goes to the forest of asceticism. What can we say about this?

body.text: (5.10) puruṣapratibhākṛtaṃ hi yadi sādhanatvaṃ syāt tadā na kiñcit sādhanamasādhanaṃ vā / sa ca heturyadi svabhāvatastaddharmabhāvī tadā kathamanyathā kriyeta? vastusvabhāvānyathābhāvasyābhāvāt / ekasya ca viruddhobhayasvabhāvasyābhāvāt / ataddharmabhāvī ca kathamanyadāpi sādhanaṃ kasyacit / tasmāt svabhāvataḥ svasvasādhyāvinābhāvinoryathoktalakṣaṇayoḥ kāryasvabhāvahetvoḥ tallakṣaṇasya pratihetorasaṃbhavādalakṣaṇamekasaṃkhyāvivakṣā, vyavaccedyābhāvāt /
body.translated_text: (5.10) For if the status of being a proof depended on a person's insight, then nothing would be either a proof or a non-proof. And if this reason is by nature of the nature of that property [it proves], then how could it be made otherwise? — because there is no alteration of the nature of a real entity. And since a single [entity] cannot have two contradictory natures. And if [the reason] is not of the nature of that property, then how could it ever be a proof of anything? Therefore, for the effect-reason (<s>kāryahetu</s>) and the essential-nature-reason (<s>svabhāvahetu</s>), each invariably concomitant with its own <s>sādhya</s> and possessing the characteristics as stated — because of the impossibility of a counter-reason having that [same] defining characteristic — the intention to designate a single [pseudo-reason type] is a [mere] non-defining-characteristic, due to the absence of anything to be excluded.

body.text: (5.11) jñānaṃ punarna liṅgasyātmarūpamiti kathaṃ liṅgalakṣaṇaṃ bhaviṣyati / kiṃrūpād hetoranumeyo 'rtho jñātavya iti cintāyāṃ pratipatturavisaṃvādakalingasvarūpamabhidhīyate yasya darśanād ayaṃ pravibhāgena sādhanaṃ vyavasthāpya tasyeṣṭārthasaṃnidhānasaṃpratyayāt pravṛttimavalambate / tathā yadasyātmarūpaṃ tallakṣaṇaṃ na tu pararūpam / pratipattijanmani upayogamātrāt tallakṣaṇatve prameyapuruṣādīnāmapi tallakṣaṇatvaṃ bhavet / na hi teṣvapi asatsu liṅgini jñānaṃ bhavati /
body.translated_text: (5.11) Now, cognition (<s>jñāna</s>) is not the intrinsic nature of the logical mark (<s>liṅga</s>) — so how will it become the defining characteristic of the logical mark? When the question is 'from what kind of reason should the object to be inferred be known?' — the intrinsic nature of the logical mark that does not deceive the cognizer is described, [that nature] upon seeing which the person, having established the proof through discrimination, undertakes activity based on the confidence that the desired object is present. Thus, that which is the intrinsic nature of [the logical mark] is its defining characteristic, not the nature of something else. For if [something were] the defining characteristic merely because of its utility in the production of the cognition [of the cognizer], then even the object to be known (<s>prameya</s>), the person, and the like would also be defining characteristics [of the logical mark]. For without those either, cognition does not arise in the one who possesses the logical mark.

body.text: (5.12) niścitagrahaṇaṃ tarhi na kartavyam / na, tasyānyārthatvāt / sapakṣavipakṣayordarśanādarśanamātrato gamakaṃ hetumiccatāṃ naiva samartho heturbhavati satorapi darśanādarśanayoragamakatvadarśanāt / tena bhāvābhāvābhyāmeva gamako heturiti jñāpanārtha niścitagrahaṇam / tena pararūpaṃ liṅgasya lakṣaṇaṃ na bhavati, tena liṅgasya rūpaviśeṣānamidhānāt / tau hi bhāvābhāvau tadbhāvasādhakapramāṇavṛttyā boddhavyau, upāyāntarābhāvāt /
body.translated_text: (5.12) [Objection:] Then the qualification 'ascertained' (<s>niścita</s>) should not be included. — [Reply:] No, because it serves a different purpose. For those who desire a reason that serves as a means of understanding merely from [its] observation and non-observation in the homogeneous (<s>sapakṣa</s>) and heterogeneous (<s>vipakṣa</s>) [instances], the reason is never competent — since even when observation and non-observation exist, they are seen to be non-indicative. Therefore, the qualification 'ascertained' is for the purpose of making known that the reason serves as a means of understanding only through [the establishment of] presence and absence [of the invariable relation]. By this, the other's definition of the logical mark (<s>liṅga</s>) is not [accepted], since that [definition] does not designate the specific nature of the logical mark. For those two — presence and absence — are to be understood through the operation of the <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid cognition) that establishes their [invariable] connection, because there is no other means.

body.text: (5.13) yadyapi bhāvābhāvavacanamātreṇa tatsādhanapramāṇavṛttiḥ ākṣipyate, anyathā tayoreva sattā prasiddheḥ, jñānasattānibandhanatvājjñeyasattāvyavasthāyāḥ iti sarvatra jñeyasattāvyavasthaiva tatsādhanaṃ pramāṇamākarṣatiḥ parārthatvācca śāstrapraṇayanasyaḥ trirūpaṃ liṅgaṃ saṃvādakamiti tadrūpamapratipattṛṇāṃ tataḥ pravṛttirna bhavatīti paropalakṣaṇātvādeva pravartake jñānaṃ siddhamḥ tathāpi tāveva viśiṣṭau bhāvābhāvau kecid darśanādarśanamātreṇa vyavasthāpayantīti teṣāṃ niṣedhārtho 'yaṃ niścitaśabdaḥ prayuktaḥ / satorapi bhāvābhāvadarśanayoḥ anvayavyatirekayoḥ saṃśayāt / tasmāt pratibandhasādhakapramāṇavṛttyaiva bhāvābhāvau sidhyata iti vipratipattinirāsārthamasmābhirniścitagrahaṇaṃ kṛtam /
body.translated_text: (5.13) Although the operation of the <s>pramāṇa</s> that establishes that [invariable relation] is implied by the mere statement of presence and absence — because otherwise the mere existence of those two would be well-known [without any special <s>pramāṇa</s>], since the determination of the existence of the knowable depends on the existence of knowledge — therefore, the very determination of the knowable's existence everywhere draws [i.e., implies] the <s>pramāṇa</s> that establishes it. And since the composition of the treatise is for others' benefit, the triple-marked logical mark (<s>liṅga</s>) is an informant [to others]; and for those who do not understand its [triple] nature, valid inference does not arise from it — therefore, cognition is established [as relevant] precisely because the [treatise] is characterized as being for others' benefit in motivating [understanding]. Nevertheless, some establish those very qualified presence and absence by mere observation and non-observation — and this word 'ascertained' (<s>niścita</s>) is employed for the purpose of negating their [position]. Because even when the observation of presence and absence, i.e., positive and negative concomitance (<s>anvaya-vyatireka</s>), exists, there is doubt [about the invariable relation]. Therefore, presence and absence are established only through the operation of the <s>pramāṇa</s> that establishes the necessary connection (<s>pratibandha</s>) — for the purpose of removing this disagreement, the qualification 'ascertained' has been employed by us.

body.text: yato 'pi trairūpyavacanamātreṇa tatsādhanapramāṇākṣepasiddhiḥ, na jñānaṃ pṛthagato rūpāntaraṃ bhavati, tenaivāvagatatvād, upalayārthavat pakṣadharmatvāt /
body.translated_text: Since even by the mere statement of the triple mark (<s>trairūpya</s>), the establishment through implication of the <s>pramāṇa</s> that proves it is [already] achieved, cognition is not a separate additional mark — because it is already understood through that very [triple mark], being a property of the thesis-subject (<s>pakṣadharma</s>), like the purpose of apprehension.

body.text: (5.14) anvayavyatirekayorapi tarhi na pṛthakatvam, ekasya prayogādubhayagateriti cet / na / hetoḥ sapakṣāsapakṣayorbhāvābhāvau na parasparamākṣipataḥ / ekaṃ vākyamubhayaṃ gamayatītyucyate naiko 'rthaḥ svabhāvo dvitīyasyeti / nanu tatraiva bhāva ityatra tadarthatayā tadabhāve 'bhāvo gamyate, atadbhāve 'vaśyamabhāva ityatra ca tadbhāve bhāva iti parasparākṣepa iti cet / vacanametat sāmarthyādubhayamākṣipati ekasyāpi niyamakhyāpakasya dvitīyākṣepanāntarīyakatvāt / na ca tāvatobhayorekasvabhāvatā / pṛthagabhidhānaṃ tu prayoganiyamārtham / na punaḥ kevalau bhāvābhāvau parasparamākṣipataḥ / niyamavantau ca na kevalau niyamasyobhayarūpatvāt /
body.translated_text: (5.14) [Objection:] Then there would be no separateness of positive and negative concomitance (<s>anvaya-vyatireka</s>) either, since from the application of one, both are obtained. — [Reply:] No. The presence and absence of the reason in the homogeneous and heterogeneous [instances] do not mutually imply each other. [Objection:] It is said that a single statement conveys both — not that a single meaning is the nature of the second. — [Reply:] But since 'presence there alone' implies 'absence in the absence of that,' and 'necessarily absence in the absence of that' implies 'presence in its presence' — there is mutual implication. — [Reply:] The statement implies both through its capacity, because even a single statement that announces restriction necessarily implies the second. But that does not make the two of one nature. Separate statement is for the purpose of restricting application. But mere presence and absence by themselves do not mutually imply each other. And restricted [presence and absence] are not mere [presence and absence], because restriction is of the nature of both.

body.text: (5.15) tasmāt tatraiva bhāva iti na bhāva evocyate itareṇāpi nā bhāva eva yena bhāvo 'bhāvo vā dvitīyamākṣipet / naivaṃ jñānaṃ, paropalakṣaṇaśāstrāgṛhītajñānāt trailakṣaṇyādavyatirekāditi na lakṣaṇāntaram / tasmātra hetuḥ ṣaḍlakṣaṇaḥ / hetubindurācāryadharmakīrtikṛtaḥ samāptaḥ /
body.translated_text: (5.15) Therefore, 'presence there alone' does not state mere presence, nor does the other [statement] state mere absence — by which presence or absence would imply the second. Cognition is not [a separate mark] in this way either — because it does not differ from the three marks, since it is not grasped by the treatise characterized as being for others' benefit as [something] separate from the three marks, and because of its inseparability from the triple characterization (<s>trailakṣaṇya</s>). Therefore, the reason here does not have six marks. The <s>Hetubindu</s> (A Drop of Reasons) composed by <s>Ācārya Dharmakīrti</s> is complete.
